speechtext: BRODEUR (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 158) respecting Meaford Harbour. He said : The object of the Bill is to legalize a situation which has existed for some years and has created some disturbance. The township of St. Vincent was at first the authority which had the power to deal with this harbour which is on Georgian bay. Later on, in 1874, if I remember well, the town of Meaford was incorporated with the harbour within its territorial limits. The municipal authorities of the town assumed that the fact that the harbour was within the boundaries of the town gave them sufficient authority to deal with the harbour, to make necessary improvements and to levy taxes. I understand that some work had been carried out by the municipality on this assumption that they were acting within their right. As some doubt has been raised as to their right to carry out these works and levy taxes, they have approached the department and asked that legislation be introduced to legalize what has been done and to declare that for the future, the harbour shall be vested in the town of Meaford.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

1.	No trap-net licenses were issued in this district in 1906.
When the decision of the Imperial Privy Council on the Fisheries Reference secured to the provincial governments the property interests in the fisheries, which involved the issue of leases and licenses for fishing privileges, it declared the clause empowering the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to issue licenses, to be ultra vires, where the right already existed by law.
The department, however, by tacit admission and tentative arrangement with the local government continued to issue licenses as formerly, pending final settlement of the question.

A gradual disposition grew up among the fishermen in this district to interpret the law for themselves and to fish trap-nets without licenses, and eventually a decision was rendered in the county court denying the right of this department to issue such licenses, which strengthened the hands of the fishermen in their contentions.
The department held, however, that subsection 7 of section 47 of the Fisheries Act, chapter 45 of the revised statutes, was to be interpreted as a prohibition of a method of fishing, not necessarily involving the abstract question of proprietary rights ; but merely giving the minister authority under certain conditions to legalize the operation of a trap-net, which was prohibited by the Act without his permission, whereas section 8 authorizing the minister to grant licenses as such, essayed to take power of a proprietary character.
Hence while he may not grant a license in the proprietary sense of the word, he could by special license or permission authorize a trap-net license, which trap could not be legally operated without his authority.
In 1906 the fishermen did not take out licenses, and early in 1907 the officer asked what course he was to follow for that year, and he was instructed to compel the fishermen to take out licenses, or remove their trap-nets with the assistance of one of the fishery protection cruisers.

Rt. bon. Sir WILFRID LAURIER (Prime Minister) moved :
That the memorandum of the Chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Commissioners to the Prime Minister, of date the 23rd April, and laid on the table of this House on the 24th instant, and the papers accompanying the same, be referred to a special committee of five members, with instructions to investigate the matters and charges therein mentioned, and that the said committee be composed of Messrs: Carvell, Macdonald (PiCtou), Geoffrion, Barker and Lennox, and that the committee have power to send for persons, papers and records.

There should also be power given to the committee to examine witnesses on oath or affirmation as otherwise the committee would have no power to do so. I would suggest further if it is the intention to deal with all the matters and charges which have been put forward in the statements purporting to emanate from Major Hodgins which have appeared in the public press, that it should be so stated in the resolution. I observe that the memo, which has been placed upon the table of the House from the chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Commission refers to an article contained in the Manitoba ' Free Press ' and a similar article in the Ottawa ' Citizen.' In the press of British Columbia the statements of Major Hodgins were set out at very considerable length and in very considerable detail, so much so that the observations of the chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Commission as to their vague and indefinite character would not seem to apply, because I observe that the Vancouver ' World,' after referring to the great weight which the words of Major Hodgins would carry in the province of British Columbia, uses this language :
We do not know that more serious oharges of robbery of the public treasury have ever been brought before the public of Canada.
There are no general statements made on hearsay, but specific allegations which can be proved or disproved, put forward by a man thoroughly familiar with the circumstances.
I would suggest therefore to the right hon. gentleman that there should be added to the resolution after the words ' therein mentioned' -on the last line of the resolution as it appears on page 10 of the Order Paper, these words :
Or set forth in the statements purporting to emanate from Major A. E. Hodgins which have appeared in the public press.
These should be added so that we may be sure, in sending the matter to the committee that we are dealing with all the charges and matters which have been alleged by this gentleman who has occasioned the action which the Prime Minister has taken.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do no.t know that I would be justified at this moment in enlarging the motion which I have just brought to the attention of the House. The action which I have taken was upon the suggestion of my hon. friend who drew my attention to this matter, and we took action upon the reports which were available at that time. If there is any thing more it ought to be a matter for further consideration. I have never even seen the newspapers to which my hon. friend refers. -

I am not asking for any thing more to be Introduced. In bringing the matter to the attention of the Prime Minister I referred to statements made in newspapers in eastern Canada, which as I understand summarized the statements made by Major Hodgins and which had appeared at greater length and in greater detail in the press of British Columbia. All that I am now suggesting is that the motion should be so framed as to include all the matters and charges which were actually mentioned or made and which were referred to but not set out in the press of eastern Canada.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly, any statement that has been made though not actually stated in detail ought to be taken in, and as I understand it myself at all events, it is being included in the resolution.

All I am in doubt about is whether or not the newspaper clippings attached to the communication from Mr. Parent contain the actual statements and charges put forward by Major Hodgins in British Columbia. In order to make that perfectly sure I was suggesting an amendment, not with the idea of adding any thing further but merely with a desire of including all the charges and statements that were actually made before I brought the matter to the attention of the government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The intention of the motion is certainly to deal with all the charges of Major Hodgins.

Would the Prime Minister be good enough to look at the motion and see whether he is quite sure of that.
Sir WILFRID* LAURIER. Not having seen the paper I am sorry that I cannot express any opinion at the moment. Perhaps I had better allow the matter to stand until to-morrow.
I can furnish to the Prime Minister some British Columbia papers which contain the statement as originally made ; he could look over these and see whether all these matters are covered.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

Hon. SYDNEY FISHER (Minister of Agriculture) moved third reading of Bill (No. 149) to amend the Meat and Canned Foods Act.
I would like to ask the minister if he intends by this Bill to do away with the name of the packer on the label. I understand that is the intention of the Bill.

I think the hon. gentleman's way of putting it is far too sweeping. It does not necessarily do away with the name of the packer, but it does permit the first purchaser from the packer to put his name on the label instead of the packer.
Then I may tell the minister that is the greatest mistake he ever made.
I did not make it. It was an amendment moved in committee, not by me, and adopted by the House.

It seems a pity to put laws on this statute-book one year and change them the next year, when they are proper laws. The canning industry in this country is a large industry and is likely to increase. It seems to me there would be no object in improving the quality of the goods unless the name of the packer is on the label, and it certainly protects the consumer. I have some special labels here which I will send over to the minister so that he may see them. We do not object to a special label but I believe the name of the packer should be on the label in every case. Some times these goods are sent out and they change hands two or three times and if the name of the packer is not on it is a very easy thing for the man behind the counter to say even unintention-Mr. R. L. BORDEN
ally they were packed by a certain firm when such might not be the case. In the interest of the business I would regret very much to see this change take place for I believe it would be a setback to the trade. I hope the minister will consider that well. We have no objection to the wholesale trade using special labels but we think the name of the packer is the best protection to the consumer. The Act of last year which provided that the name of the packer should be on the label was a good Act, and I was in sympathy with it and I regret now that it is proposed to change it. Speaking on behalf of the Canadian canners I may tell you that we are not sending 1,000 cases to the old country to-day except those which contain our own label and I say that is the best advertisement that the canned goods of this country can have. I again urge that the law should provide that the name of the packer should be on the label, if only for the purpose of protecting the consumer.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Marshall) has not advanced one argument why the respectable and responsible Canadian wholesale dealers who have advertised and established the reputation of their labels for the past thirty years should not be allowed to use them as in the past. I can readily understand that the Canadian canners which the hon. gentleman represents would derive very great advantage from a law which provided that the name of the canner should be on the label. Now, the first object and design of this law is to protect the public. That is the object of the Act. The wholesale dealers -always had canneries of their own until of late years when they have sold them out to the Canadian canners who have some thirty-five or forty canneries under their company at the present time. Two or three of these canneries have worked up great names for themselves in the past, but the public have no guarantee that they are getting the goods of these particular canneries even when they ask for them ; the Canadian canners can take the canned goods of any of their canneries and place on them the name of the favourite cannery.
As to the question of responsibility, we know that the wholesale grocers are among the most substantial business concerns in Canada, much more responsible than many of the small packers. If the wholesale grocers are compelled to put the name of the canners on the goods, the effect would be to practically wipe out the whole business of the small canner as it would not pay the wholesale dealer to have his labels printed except in large quantity, and if the name of the cannery must be put on, then the wholesaler would practically be compelled to purchase his goods from the Canadian canners. In the past the wholesale

grocers have bought their canned goods from perhaps a dozen different canneries under their own special supervision. They are bound to have their goods of the very highest quality, and when the wholesale grocers put their own names on the cans it is a guarantee to the public that they are getting first class goods.
May I ask the hon. gentleman a question ? The hon. gentleman is entirely wrong when he says-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not a question, that is the statement of fact.
Does the hon. member know of his own knowledge that these special brands have been in use for 20 or 30 years ?
I do.
Name the label ?
I am not prepared to name the label.
I thought you were not.
Rut I know and you know that such firms as Balfour & Company, James Turner & Company, of Hamilton, have used their labels for many years.

I do not know that and I am correct when I say that these special labels have not been used longer than seven years. I have the dates when their use was commenced, I know what I am talking about. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Zimmerman) does not really understand it; they have not been using these labels for twenty or thirty years. I am speaking of fruit and vegetable labels.
Mr. Speaker

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Marshall) should not interrupt another member who has the floor except with his consent. That is the rule.
The system of labels that have been used by the wholesale grocers-

I would like to ask another question. In which way would the public be most protected, by having the name of the canner, the man who packs the goods, or the name of the wholesale dealer on the packages ?

Unquestionably by having the name of the wholesale dealer. The wholesale trade have established a large business all over the country in their special brands or labels and the system has worked well. They have spent large sums of money on these labels and to require that the name of the packer should be placed on the can practically means confiscation of one of the most valuable assets of the wholesale grocer.
220J
Is the hon. gentleman aware that the canners allow the cost of these labels when they puc them on ? The wholesale man is not at the loss of the labels.
I am aware that they allow a certain percentage. That is not the point.
I understood his argument to be there was a great loss on the labels.

No, I say the loss would be in the confiscation of a valuable advertised asset, an asset on which the wholesale grocer has worked up a large business during many years. That business has been established on a particular label, the trade have been well satisfied with the goods they have received, and now if you compel the name of the canner to go on these packed goods, it simply means confiscation of the wholesale grocers' most valuable asset.
Does it make any serious difference if you place on the label : Canned by so and so for such a wholesale firm ?
Certainly, as practically every wholesale grocer would have to go to the Canadian canners to get his goods and they would be practically selling the same goods.

The hon. gentleman is entirely mistaken ; they would not have to go to the Canadian canners, for there are more goods packed outside of Canadian canners than they are packing. Why do they want these special labels put on certain packages ? Because these goods have been before the public and have a reputation. When they send in their orders to the Canadian canners, they say : We want them labelled as packed at Aylmer-or some other point where the goods have a reputation.

Then why does the new packer always want to use his own

label ? Is it not because be wishes to get established, to get his goods out ? It is the new packer who wants to use his own label.

All I can say is that the present system has been very satisfactory so far as concerns getting goods put up by_ the wholesale grocers under their own private labels. It has worked well, the public have been protected, the policy has been successful and under it a large special business has been worked up. It has also enabled the small packers to establish a successful business. If you insist on the packer's name going on all these goods, it is no more protection to the consumer than having the name of the wholesale grocer on them, and it means confiscation of one of the most valuable assets of the wholesale grocer in his special label.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken entirely.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has exercised his right to speak on this motion.
I have had the floor

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman has also exercised nis right.

It seems to me that the hon. member for East Elgin, for whose opinion in this matter I have every possible regard, is unnecessarily alarmed over this suggested amendment. The section provides that these articles shall be marked with :
(a) The initials of the Christian names, the full surname, and the address, or, in the case of a firm or corporation, the firm or corporate name and address, of the packer.
and the amendment comes in here :
Or of the first dealer obtaining it direct from the packer who sells or offers the same for .sale. Such dealer shall, upon request of the inspector, disclose the name of the packer of such article.
Let me tell my hon. friend (Mr. Marshall) the reason for this amendment. I received from the Wholesale Grocers' Guild of the province of British Columbia a resolution passed at the last meeting, pointing out that the majority of them had been operating on specific labels more particularly for canned salmon. For a number of years, it has been the custom for the wholesaler' to go to a small packer of salmon and purchase his output. The packer does not label the goods, but they are labelled by the wholesaler with his own brand, and the wholesaler assumes full responsibilty for the purity of the article, and is held responsible under this amendment. Without this amendment, the packer would be obliged to put his name on the can. Now, John Jones
may have been the packer last year
I think canned fish does not come under the operation of this section.
Fish is subject to the provisions of the law under section 12.

I was pointing out that the wholesale dealer puts his label on the can. For instance, a man deals in what he calls the 'Sunset' brand of-canned salmon, using that brand for years and buying his canned salmon, possibly, from four or five different canners. This is necessary for the reason that a good run of salmon in a certain river one year may mean a poor run next year, making it necessary for the wholesaler to go to a different part of British Columbia for his canned salmon next year. '

I understand you to say that he would not be able to use the same packer, and so his labels would' be a loss. But you could overcome that by putting on a narrow strip ' packed by so and so ' upon the label.

My hon. friend and I are working on the same lines ; we want somebody held responsible for the quality of the goods. But this is not a question of changing a label, but it is a question of maintaining a dealer's right in his own brand. A man may have built up a reputation for a certain brand of canned salmon. Under the present Act, he cannot operate in that way. Last year, for instance, the salmon was packed by John Jones ; this year it is packed by Smith and Brown. Cans thus differently marked might be put upon the same shelf, and my hon. friend will understand that this is a position that the wholesale grocers of British Columbia desire to escape. And I think that their position in the matter is very laudable and very fair.
Are all the wholesale people in British Columbia in sympathy with this ?
Yes.
Are you not mistaken in that ?
1 have received a letter from the Wholesale Grocers' Guild of British Columbia on the subject. I am sorry I have not that letter with me-
The reason I ask is that one wholesale house in Vancouver particularly did not want this.

There may be one firm. But I have had several letters on the subject, including the one of which I speak, from the Secretary of the Wholesale Grocers' Guild which comprises practically all the wholesale dealers in British Columbia. Of course, my hon. friend wil understand that I am not working for any particular

grocer. I know that the wholesale grocers will be placed at a disadvantage or compelled to operate under the present section 12 of the Act.

I would like to ask the hon. gentleman a question :	If you
were buying a case of Cross & Blackwell's goods, or of Heinz's or of Snider's ketchup, would not you want to see their names on the goods ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would remind hon. members in speaking, they must address the chair.
I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, but it is hard for me, apparently, to make myself clear, and this is a very important question.

My hon. friend (Mr. Marshall) is right. If I asked for Crosse & Blackwell's goods, I would want to get what I asked for. Why ? Because, in the course of a long period of years, they have built up a reputation for their goods.

Well, here is a company that has been packing for twenty-four or twenty-five years. We have a reputation for our goods and do not want to give it away. Our position is just the same as that of Crosse & Blackwell.
I appreciate that. You put your label on the goods. You do not send out your goods under-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member (Mr. Macpherson) is doing exactly what I objected to a moment ago.

I beg pardon of the House. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Marshall) does simply what the wholesale grocers of British Columbia are doing. If I know anything of the canning industry of Canada, I know that the people who have established a reputation for their labels desife to have their brands maintained. My hon. friend suggested that if I ask for Crosse & Blackwell's goods I want them. Yes, and if I ask for the Clover Leaf brand of salmon, I want it, irrespective of the identity of the actual packer. It does not matter that it has been packed by one firm and labelled by another. The firm that labels the good's is as desirous of keeping its business intact and not letting anybody else know where they get this canned salmon as Crosse & Blackwell are to keep people from infringing on their label. But my hon. friend will see that the present Act makes that impossible. I cannot see how any harm could accrue to the man who buys or to the canner, through this amendment relating to the ' first dealer.'
But the harm is to the consumer, and it is the consumer we want to protect.

I took the staud last year that there should be the name of some responsible party upon the canned salmon. Until last year there was no responsible name upon the canned salmon, because, in many instances, the goods were packed, labelled and sent out without any individual name on the can.
As the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macpherson) reads the amendment, is it clear that the canner's label may be on the can or that of the first purchaser ?
Yes.
Would the first purchaser be authorized to tear off the label of the packer and put on his own ?
I fancy that he would ecme under the operation of the criminal code if he attempted to do that. Of course, I am not a lawyer.
This would seem to authorize it.
I do not think so. But the point I am trying to bring out-and I am sorry that this is not in committee, for I would like my hon. friend from Elgin to have the fullest opportunity for discussing it
Section 18 provides against the difficulty suggested by the hon. member for Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn).

Section 18 says :
Every person who, not being an inspector, wilfully ajters. effaces, or obliterates, or causes to be altered, effaced or obliterated, wholly or partially, anv mark on any article which has undergone inspection shall incur a penalty of one hundred dollars.
That, I fancy, would cover. But what I am trying to point out is that the man who has established a reputation for a brand of canned salmon finds that brand practically wiped out under this law unless he can go into the canning business himself. If he is not in a position to do so, but goes into the open market, buys a pack of canned salmon, has it inspected and has his label put on it, that is a guarantee that the article is sound and fit for food.

As I understand it, there may be a failure of the catch, so that the dealer is not able to procure his supply from the same packer as in a former year, and may even be compelled to buy from two or three packers. What guarantee is there to the public that these different packs of salmon are equally good when they are packed without the direct supervision of the wholesale men ?

Of course, the wholesale man comes under the operation of this Act. The wholesale purchaser is

going to be very careful, because he has established a reputation for his goods. He will see that nothing but the very best goods go out under his name. The hon. gentleman will understand that a man who has been putting up a particular kind of goods under a patent name, if he puts out an inferior article for only one year, it will injure the reputation of his goods for all time.
How do you determine that they are up to the standard?

There is a physical way of doing so. All canned salmon are inspected by a provincial officer in British Columbia. I went with him last year through some of the canneries, and saw some of the salmon condemned. The man who purchases has no trouble at all in ascertaining the character of the salmon by opening a can. The operation of canning salmon is down to such a perfect science that it is almost impossible for bad salmon to be put up-except possibly in a very bad year.
Does the hon. gentleman not think that the packer would be in a better position than the grocer to say as to the quality of the contents of the package ?
They are all subject to inspection under this Act.
If they all come up to the one standard why should one be better than another?

The idea is this : If you are a wholesale grocer operating in British Columbia and you have established a reputation for a certain brand of goods, and are using your own label, naturally you will be obliged to keep your goods up to the highest possible standard. But under the present operation of the Act, you could not go to three or four different canneries and buy your whole output for that year, because in one ease you would possibly buy the pack of Jones and Brown, and in another ease the pack of Smith and Robinson, all carrying a certain class of brand.
Does ,the hon. gentleman not think that the packer would be more particular if his own name were on the package than if he sent it out without his name?

I agree that the packer is going to be very particular. But we have many small packers who don't go into the market with their canned goods ; they depend entirely upon the wholesale grocer for the sale of their goods. The hon. gentleman will understand that if the wholesale grocer is obliged to go to three or four different canners, under the present operation of this Act he is obliged to buy goods that are labelled bv three or Mr. MACPHERSON.
four different men, and if he put his own label on all those goods and sent them to eastern Canada he would soon receive a black eye.
They would have a double guarantee.

Possibly, and you cannot have the food you eat too well guaranteed. But the people have the guarantee of the responsible wholesale firm that these goods are pure, and they are also inspected by the government. They operate under this label and they are responsible for the goods.
Would the public not have the same guarantee from the manufacturer himself under the present Bill?

The question of vested rights comes in. These people have operated under this label for years, but under the strict operation of this Act they cannot operate under that label any more. Everybody has been protected under this Act, the wholesaler, the canner and the user himself. I think my bon. friend from Elgin (Mr. Marshall) is unnecessarily alarmed. I agree that we should have every possible guarantee, but there can be no better guarantee than is here provided. There are many reputable wholesale grocery firms in this country whose names are synonymous for purity of goods and for fair dealing. They have operated in British Columbia for thirty or forty years under one specific label, but buying from several different factories. How unfair it would be if the vested rights of these men in their labels were wiped out, and only the packer's name should be allowed to go on the label.
How long has the canning business been in operation in this country ?

I know they have been canning fish for thirty-three years, I withdraw the words forty years. In 1877 salmon were first canned in the Fraser river. It is a question of the vested rights that a wholesale grocer has in his patent label. He has been protected by this law, and the wholesale packer is not being at all molested.

Who has the most money invested in this business, is it the man who supplies the label, or the man who builds a plant to put up the goods ? We do not object to special labels, but we want the packer's name to be on the label. We will put on any label they require, but we say that in the interest of the builder, and to protect the consumer, the name of the packer should be on.

My hon. friend has got the wrong side of my argument. It is not a question of a label, the printing

of a label does not amount to much money; but it is a question of the vested rights of a man in goods that he has packed and sold for years. The person whose name is on the label is the man who is responsible under present conditions.

British Columbia methods in the canning business must differ from those obtaining in Ontario. The business in Ontario has not been in operation for thirty or forty years, and it is impossible for the wholesale men to have acquired any such vested rights as the hon. gentleman has referred to. In Ontario the canned goods business has only been in operation for about twenty years. When the packer of the goods has placed his own label on a package, in the lapse of years that label has acquired a large money value, and it appears to me that the effort now being made to place somebody else's label on the goods ought not to succeed. It would deprive the packers of this country of the large value that they have acquired in their labels. The hon member for Hamilton speaks of the responsibility of firms. This matter of labels being placed by wholesale firms on packers' goods, is a matter of recent years. The person responsible for the contents of the can is surely the packer who has placed his label on those goods. The hon. gentleman says that the label is for the protection of the public. Well, he argues in a circle. Ever since the business has been in existence the canner has placed his label upon the goods. The public have learned to value the goods by their acquaintance with these labels placed upon them by the canners. The labels put on by the "wholesale men are a matter of recent years, and their value cannot be as great. The hon. gentleman evidently sees the force of that statement, and knows that the facts are as I have stated, because he adds that the wholesale dealers have in some instances established a canning business and have built It up, and says the public will be protected in getting the particular goods of these firms. That is precisely the case as I have put it. But the canners are the people who have the original vested rights. If there is any question of vested rights involved in this matter, it is the rights of the canner who, by lapse of time, has acquired a priority in such rights. They made the business. There was a time when there was no canning business in this country. The canners are the people who have made the business, spent the money, established the plants, gained a reputation for the goods they manufacture and established the value of their labels by trading with the public. Now, the wholesale dealers are endeavouring to take away that value which has been built up by long years of effort.
It is just the reverse.

The hon. gentleman speaks of the wholesalers being the people who are responsible for the quality of the goods. How can they possibly give any guarantee of the quality of goods bought from a dozen different sources?
They have all to be subject to the same inspection.

But there was a time when there was no inspection and when they bought the goods absolutely on the reputation of the packer. That is the reputation that the public desire to rely upon. They have learned to know these labels, they have learned to know the relative value of the goods, and they will be unfamiliar with the new labels put on by the wholesale men. The member for Vancouver (Mr. Macpherson) says that it is a question of vested rights. I say: Yes, the vested rights of the packer. Surely the packers are the people who were on the scene first, they are the people who originated the business, and this is an attempt of the wholesaler to come in and take the benefit of the packers' years of work. I would certainly oppose in the strongest possible manner any amendment to the Act or any legislation which would have the effect of depriving the packer of the right to the full use of his labels and of his name for the purpose of placing his goods before the public. The public are entitled to the labels, they are acquainted with the reputation of the packer, these labels have a high money value to the packer and that money value ought not to be disturbed.

I beg to move, seconded by the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Win. Jackson):
That Bill No. H9 be not now read the third time but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole for further consideration.
I suppose there will be no objection to allowing this Bill to go back to Committee of the Whole. There must be a considerable difference of opinion as to whether the Bill is a correct one or not, and I think it is a matter that the minister will consent to at once.
I do not think this Bill ought to go back to Committee of the Whole. If any hon. members do not approve of any portion of the Bill they may move to strike out that clause.
No, this is the third reading.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The only recourse is to move to refer it back.

Mi'. FISHER. If the hon. member wishes to refer it back for a particular purpose I would not object at all.
It is for a particular purpose.
But that is not mentioned in the motion; the motion is simply that the Bill be referred back to the Committee of the Whole.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: For further consideration.
It means that the whole Bill shall be referred back for consideration.
There is only one clause of the Bill that there is any difference of opinion on.

If the hon. gentleman wisnes to move that this Bill be referred back for the purpose of striking out this particular amendment I have no objection, but if it is proposed to refer the whole Bill back for further consideration I would object.
For the purpose of considering the amendment. It may not be desired to strike it out altogether, but to modify it in some way.
That particular amendment?
Yes, that is the only one we are discussing; refer it back for the purpose of further considering that clause, whatever it is.
It is an amendment to clause 12.
Do you object to that?

I do not object to it. I am willing that the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Marshall) shall have every possible chance to express his views; still, I think he is entirely mistaken.
And the amendment proposed is as follows:
Or of the first dealer obtaining it direct from the packer who sells or offers the same for sale. Such dealer shall, upon request of the inspector, disclose the name of the packer of such article.

Mr. Chairman, this is the clause striking the name of the packer from the label. I am anxious to have the name of the packer put on the label. I want to say a few words about the label. The hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Zimmerman) said that some of these labels had been used for a number of years. I have the dates here showing the periods for which some of them have been used. The ' Triangle ' commenced to be used three years ago. The ' Tartan ' brand is the oldest in use, this label having been originated seven years ago. I am speaking only of fruit and vegetable labels.
Are those a manufacturer's label or a wnolesaler's label?

These are what we call special labels. Every one of these labels has the name of the packer. I do not think that the Canadian canners are going to pack all these goods. They could not do it. I am speaking in the interest of the business. I am interested largely in the canned. goods business, and I am anxious to work up the quality of our goods. There is no reason why we should not be packing all the vegetables and catsups consumed in this country. There is nothing, to my mind, that will improve the quality of these goods more than putting our labels on them.

The wholesale groc ers do not object to the canners' name going on the goods. The packer is not compelled to sell to the wholesale grocer who insists that the name of the packer shall not be on the label.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The motion, as I understand it, is:
That Bill No. 149 be not now read the third time but that it be referred back to the Committee of the Whole for the purpose of further considering the amendment to clause 12.
Motion agreed to, and House went agaiii into committee on the Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Section 32 of the Act provides that:
All articles prepared for food in any estab lishment and packed in cans or similar re ceptacles, or in any package whatever, shal be subject to inspection during the whole course of preparation and packing; and all such packages shall be marked with-
(a) the initials of the Christian names, the full surname and the address, or, in the case ot a firm or corporation, the firm or corporate name and address of the packer Mr. SPEAKER.
I quite understand that, but the wholesale man will come to us and say: If you do not use our special label we will not buy your goods.
You are not compelled to sell to them?

Not at all, but what we want to do is to improve the quality of the goods. The hon. member for Hamilton knows very well that when he was in the clothing business he had a reputation for clothes. I used to buy clothes from him myself, I wanted to see his name on the goods, and it was on them. He knows as well as he is sitting here that that is the proper course to take. But, some of the wholesale men are behind him; I do not know whether it is votes he is looking after or not; but he has taken a different attitude 1 from that which he took last year.

No, I have always taken the same stand on this question. It is a matter of great moment to the wholesale dealer, and I will tell the hon. gentleman that when a man has worked up a large business under a specific label or trade mark it would be an outrage to take it away from him.
It is impossible to work up a very large business in three years.
The hon. gentleman is most unfair. He knows that there are lots of labels that have been used in this country.
Mention them.

I am not in a position to mention them, but the wholesale grocers from one end of the Dominion to the other are opposed to the Bill as it stands, and they have besieged members of this House with letters appealing to them to protect their vested interests in these labels. I think it is most unfair for the hon. gentleman to take advantage of his position in this House to represent his own business while the wholesale grocers, not being members of the House, are not here to defend themselves. I do trust that the hon. gentleman will not press this matter any further because the amendment is not interfering with him.
The objection I see to the proposed amendment is that it creates a monopoly on the part of the wholesale dealer.
Not at all; it is the other way on.
That may be my hon. friend's opinion.
It is the other way on.

I have a label here which reads as follows: 'Triangle, James Turner & Co., Hamilton; put up expressly for us by the Canadian Canners', Limited.' If the amendment becomes law, James Turner & Co. will have the right to go to six different canning establishments in Canada and make an agreement for the 'Triangle' brand to go on each package.
What would be the objection?
They would not be a uniform quality of goods because they were put up by six different canneries.
But he is responsible.
The impression left on the consumer would be that all these goods w^ere canned in the one establishment, when as a matter of fact they would be canned in six different establishments.
And the Canadian canners to-day will put up the same brand in different factories.

But the canner's name would be on the label. Under the proposed legislation the wholesale man can arrange with the manufacturer, and the manufacturer's name would not go on the goods, and yet he would be responsible for the contents of the can.
The wholesale grocer is responsible.
The canner who puts up the goods is in a far better position to guarantee the contents than the wholesale dealer who never sees them.
They are all subject to the same inspection.

I appreciate what the hon. member (Mr. Marshall) says, but we must not forget that it is the practice all over the world for large wholesale houses to have private brands. If that be the practice in England, in Germany, in France and in the United States, there is good reason for favourably considering that we should follow it in this young country. One reason why the wholesale grocer wants his private brand is that when the brand is established he has control of his trade. Under other conditions a competitor may come in and quote the same brand, if it is not a special brand, at 2j cents a dozen less, and the impression is given that all the other goods sold by that man are sold at a lesser rate than the competitor sells them at. That may be unfair competition. It is most important in the interest of the large packers generally that their brands should go to the public and that a demand should be created for them because of their quality. But it seems to me that no great wrong can accrue to the consuming public if a wholesale house of high standing undertakes to buy these goods from the packer and put his own name on them and become responsible. He will make sure that he buys from a responsible packer.
If these goods turn out bad who is to pay for them?
As a rule the wholesale grocer must make good to the retail grocer, the retail grocer must make good to the consumer, and the packer is supposed to guarantee his goods for six months.
You are perfectly right, but suppose the wholesale man uses a special label on three or four dfferent packs how can you adjust the claims if the name of the packer is not on the label ?
Every packer has a box mark and every package of goods is identified by the case.
Yes, but some retail men take tbe goods out of the different cases as soon as they receive them, put them on the shelves and sell or destroy the case.

That may be true, and it is not an exceptional way of doing business. We have not. however, had such a stringent law as is now proposed except during the past year, and I think we can fairly well take the risk we have taken for so many years. I realize it is important to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Marshall) that his goods should go to the consuming public under his own name, but is that any Teason why some other packer who may not be as able as he is to do that should not be allowed to make a bargain with some large distributing house to put on their own label and be responsible to the consuming public?
Would it not he fairer for that other packer to put his own brand on his own goods ?
There is nothing to prevent him from doing so.
But it allows the wholesaler who is not a packer to use a label which would lead the public to believe that he put up the goods.
That is quite true, but all the same he has worked up a trade under that special brand and one reason for the special brand is that it prevents competition from another wholesale grocer.
Upon what principle of *right or equity should a wholesale dealer be allowed to build up a value out of the goods of a canner who has created the value by his label being on these goods ?
He may not have created the value at all. It may be that it is the facilities which the wholesale man has for distributing the goods that creates the value.

The canners of Ontario are not depending on the wholesale trade for a market for their goods. There is one very large cannery in my county which deals with no wholesaler, keeps no travellers upon the road, sells their -whole pack annually to one or two dealers in the larger centres and could sell them five times the amount if they had them.
I can quite believe that. This is not a question of canners and canners so far as I am concerned.
That is what it seems to be developing into.

My hon. friend is making it that. The canner has every right to place his name on the can. but the small canner who does not put his Mr. LOGGIE.
label on the goods has only the wholesale firms to look to for distributing them. The small mau is protected in his interest. The hon. member says that some canners will never go to the wholesale house. The same thing occurs in the fish business, a certain brand of salmon that I have in mind will sell anywhere.
I cited that to show the value of the brand of that company. Those goods are sold upon that brand and upon nothing else.
Exactly and that is the reason I desire to have an amendment providing that the man who has established a brand but who is not a packer shall not have his label wiped out.

What about the canner who has used his brand for a number of
years ?
This does not interfere with him. If I pack fish and desire to put my name on, this does not prevent me.
Suppose the wholesale man covers the packer's name with his label.
Then he comes under the criminal code and goes to jail, which is tile proper place for him.
The hon. gentleman seems to think I am speaking entirely for the company in which I am interested.
I do not think so.

I am interested in the canned goods business, I am anxious to improve the quality ; I know what that means; immediately we get our standard up we can sell our goods. I want to stop American goods coming in. There is no reason why they should come in. Some of them are of better quality than ours, but to my mind nothing will stop their importation so quickly as putting the name of the packer on the goods. It musr be remembered that there are some 40 packers outside the company in which I am interested. I am not speaking for my own company, I am speaking for the interest of the business. As a matter of fact the wholesale men have nothing invested in this business. You speak of their having so much invested, but that is not the case. This adoption of the special label is not desired by all the wholesale houses themselves ; we have letters from some of them asking me to oppose it. If you want to improve the quality of your goods be sure to have your name on. The Bill that passed last year, with some amendments, is a good Bill and I would be sorry to see it interfered with because to my mind as it stands it is a move in the right direction. This proposed new measure would be setting this business back ten or fifteen years.
Oh no.

I am speaking as a practical man; I have been in the business 25 years and my whole aim has been to improve the quality of the goods. The goods I have been manufacturing for years have gone into the hon. gentleman's city and I know he has asked for that particular brand. Why ? Because he knew the goods were right. That applies to all goods properly labelled. There is nothing that will improve the quality so qqickly as placing the name of the packer on the goods. I am not talking in the interest of my company at all. I am talking in the interest of the whole canned goods business because I think it is in its infancy in this country. When the great Northwest fills up. where to-day we have 80 canneries, we will then have 180. I am sincere in what I say and I hope this Act will not be meddled with at all. I cannot speak too strongly on this question as I realize its importance.

I accept fully my hon. friend's statements, that he is not speaking for his canneries. I would not for a moment accuse him of that, his standing in this country is too high. But I know he is unnecessarily alarmed. I know a little about canned goods myself. I cannot speak from the practical standpoint of my hon. friend, but I know that there is no better canned fruit on the continent of America to-day than the Canadian. I was in the Santa Clara valley three years ago and met the canners there one afternoon. The statement was made there that the Santa Clara people did not put up some varieties of fruit and vegetables equal to those put up in the province of Ontario by the Canadian canners. I thought that was a very high tribute to Canadian canning. They did not speak of all classes of goods, but spoke especially of the very high class of our peas, peaches, and one or two other varieties. British Columbia possibly consumes more per capita of canned goods than any other part of Canada and there the Canadian packers have worked up a trade into which the Americans cannot cut. They are not getting in to-day excepting where the Canadians cannot supply the goods, as my hon. friend from Elgin knows. In the Dawson country, where so much canned goods are used, that applies fully ; you cannot sell American goods if they can get Canadian. My hon. friend evaded the point I tried to make, I would have him understand that this amendment is as much in the interest of the small salmon packer as of the wholesaler. The small eanner does not put his label on his goods, possibly he does not want to, and nine times out of ten he does not. The large eanner does because he has his market, but the small cauner depends on the wholesale man who has perhaps handled his output for years.
Is the hon. member speaking of fruit and vegetables or fish ?
Fish entirely.
That is not the case in Ontario.

I appreciate that, the trouble is that Canada is a large country. The canners of British Columbia and of Ontario are in the same position of desiring to see good goods on the market, but what may apply to British Columbia may not apply to Ontario. That is the' point I tried to make in regard to the operation of this clause on the canners of British Columbia. It will not hurt the canners so much although it will to some extent. I am trying to protect the man who has a reputation established but who is not a eanner.
Does not my hon. friend think that the effect of this will be to increase the importation of American canned goods ?
The United States cannot get a market in the District of Columbia when the Canadian eanner can supply the goods. The hon. member for Elgin knows that.

I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken. If he goes to Bate's he will find American corn retailing at 25 cents a can. Why is that ? It is packed by Warner & Company, of Maine, and is extra fine corn. He is entirely mistaken in saying that American goods are not consumed here.
I know they are.
And they are sold at high prices. Our corn retails at 15 cents or two for a quarter, but Bate & Company are retailing American corn of the same size at 25 cents a tin.

But our corn comes into competition, it is selling at two for a quarter. The statement I make is that there are no better goods than ours manufactured on the continent. Take Alaska salmon and Rivers Inlet salmon. The Alaska salmon is cheaper to the merchant than the Rivers Inlet but he does not buy it because he knows that the Rivers Inlet salmon is a good, sound salmon ; he is not afraid to stake his reputation on it and he cannot afford to take seconds and place his label on them. We have to compete against canned goods from the American side but in the West where the consumption of canned goods is greatest, where they come in competition, the Canadian goods have shut them out of the market. They are put up in a northern climate and are generally a better class of goods, and are possibly as well tinned as the American, because the canneries are very up-to-date. I do not think there is

any danger under the present Act or this amendment of any influx of American goods.
This amendment, I understand, is introduced at the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Mae-pherson).
Yes.

My information from the west is that the chief thought of the western dealers who are in favour of this amendment is that it will give them a better opportunity to import goods from the United States.

That is a side light I have never received and that is not an argument they advanced to me. I do not think it is so, as they are obliged to . meet the Canadian tariff. And this clause does not make it any easier u get the goods in.
Does not my hon. friend think that will be the result if the amendment is passed ?

I really do not. This Act has been in operation for a year. The wholesale grocers say that section 12 has worked a hardship, and, in view of that fact, I desire to make this amendment to help them out. This Act respecting meat and canned foods is a splendid law. It was necessary in the best interest of the canner.
Do you really mean that now ?

I have always been looked upon as being fairly frank in my statements. And I must tell my hon. friend that I mean every word I have said. I may be entirely mistaken, of course. I always give credit to my hon. friend (Mr. Marshall) for sincerity, and I think he should mete out to me the same measure of charity.

I did not put it the right way. I think I know the mind of the hon. member (Mr. Macpherson) and that if he would tell the House just what he thinks about it, he would say that the label should be on. He is a practical man and knows that that is the only way to meet the case.

I agree about the placing of the label. That is the proper thing, an excellent thing ; it should be done, and will be done in nine hundred and ninety-nine cases out of a thousand. Possibly, after this law has been in operation for a few years, the men who are using the special labels will be eliminated. But this House has no desire, nor has my hon. friend (Mr. Marshall), to work a hardship on a man who has established a reputation for his label after years and years of labour.

Take, for instance, Todd & Company, large (Opjerators on the Fraser river. Suppose that the Fraser river is a failure one year. Todd & Company have entered into a contract for so many thousand cases of canned salmon for the old country market. They are so many hundreds of cases short. They buy what they need from a small cannery. They are practical men, and, of course, they see to it that the goods are right. Every can of these goods is marketed on Todd & Company's label. The present operation of the law has the effect of wiping that out. Does not the hon. gentleman (Mr. Marshall) see the force of that statement ?
The same thing applies to other caimers. The canners may go to a small independent canner and buy his output and put on it their own label and their own brand.
That is true. We do that. But what does the small packer say?" He may be only a beginner and trying to establish his own label. And he objects.
This does not prevent him from putting on his own label.

I am not speaking of the case referred to by the hon. member (Mr. Macpherson) of which I know nothing.
I know that it is the case here that we buy small packs. But we examine the goods.
That is what I say.
And our name is on the goods-the name of some packer appears on the label. It does not matter who packs the goods ; I want to see the name on the label.

This is a question of great importance. It affects three classes of people-the canner, the wholesale grocer and the public. The law that was passed last year was a step in advance. We know that the public are very skeptical about canned goods and this has affected the business, and we believe that the law passed last year will improve the business. But, if we adopt this amendment, we help to create a monopoly by giving the wholesale merchant an advantage. If the small canners wish to protect their goods by putting on their name, they should be allowed to do so. Not only that, but, under this amendment, the wholesale merchant is likely to go to the small canner and say : We want to purchase your goods, but we will not do so unless you allow us to put on our label. Why should the small catn-ner be forced to allow the wholesaler to use his own label and thus destroy the advantage of the canner ? We know that some canners do not produce as good goods as others. My hon. friend (Mr. Macpherson) suggested that Ontario produced the best,

that British Columbia did not produce always as good quality as other parts of the country.
I never said so.

The hon. gentleman said that Ontario produced the best goods. That being the case, if you facilitate the putting on of the wholesale grocer's label instead of that of the packer, the purchaser does not know1 who puts up the goods or where they come from. This tends to the putting up of goods of inferior quality, for the man who puts up the best quality is deprived of the advantage which he ought to have. The present law has not had time to work out its results, and we should be careful how we make changes. Certainly, changes should not be made at the instance of the wholesalers and at the expense of the can-tier and the consumer. It is very likely that the canners would not be so careful if they sold to the wholesaler as they would if they had to send their goods out to the world bearing their own name. And, just as soon as we find our own goods going down in quality, we find increased danger of importation from the United States and other countries. Therefore, it seems to me that the amendment, while it may be to the advantage of the wholesale grocers, is not in the interest of the canners or the public.
The hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Marshall) says he buys goods from the small canner. Does he put on the small canners' labels, or the label of the canners' association ?

It there are two or three canners under the control of one concern, that concern might put its own label on the goods. But all are equally responsible, for their interests are identical and that interest is to build up their own brand. Though doing business in three places, perhaps, they are practically one.

I still think it would be reasonable to add an amendment providing that the name of the packer should be put on the can. as well as the name of the wholesale firm that handles the product if he so ddsires it. That is often done. Then we would preserve the value of the name or reputation which the wholesale firm had built up during perhaps a long number of years, as well as the good name of the canner. Machine companies do that with reference to binder twine. The binder twine wrhich is sold in the United States by the McCormick Company, much of it is manufactured by the Binder Twine manufacturers in Canada. They send a man especially to supervise the operation when the article is being manufactured, and it is made of a superior quality. The wholesale firm may have acquired a reputation for sending out a good quality, but I do not see why the manufacturers who produce that good quality should not share in some of the benefits as well as the seller.

If the packer's name is not on the can he is not known to the

trade. The packer has his money invested in the plant, and it would not be fair to the man who has built the factory and put in the machinery if he were not allowed to put his name on the package. If we get the beneiit of publicity in putting out high class goods, we will be able to keep our plant in better condition and to put up still better goods.
The hou. gentleman said a little while ago that he bought the entire pack of small canneries; did he put the labels on each one of those canneries on the aggregate pack, or did he put his own label?
We put our own label on.
Then what is the difference between his relation to these purchased goods, and the relation of the wholesale grocer who puts his label on them?

We are packers. We only buy from other canners when we are short. We do not buy these goods to speculate on, but only when we are short in filling orders and have to look outside. But we examine the goods thoroughly before we put our label on.

I must say that I cannot see the value that is attached to the Shibboleth of a packer. The wholesaler is just as well able to judge of the quality of the goods that he did not pack as the packer himself.
We send a practical man to examine the goods before we buy them, a man who thoroughly understands canned goods.
The wholesale grocer is also able to send a practical man.
It is only practical men who are capable of judging of these goods.
The hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Marshall) knows of cases where goods were sent out from the canneries to the wholesale grocers, and were returned as not being up to the mark.

The party who buys from the original canner is responsible. We would not be responsible for the party selling, but if we get a poor quality of goods we come back upon the original packer. We are responsible because we know the brand.

I think this is a matter that should receive the special attention of the Minister of Agriculture. He introduced a Bill in 1907, it has only been on the statute-book for twelve months. A very important alteration is proposed to be made in the Bill. The minister will not father the change. He has already stated that the amendment was not proposed by himself, rather shirking the responsibility for Mr. MARSHALL.
the change, and yet I suppose he has consented that the change shall be made. I would like to direct my hon. friend's attention to the fact that whatever responsibility there is for this change will rest upon the minister himself. 1 do not think he is doing justice to the people of Canada by consenting that legislation of this kind shall take place. If this legislation is passed it will be practically impossible to follow the goods back to the door of the manufacturer. For example, James Turner & Co. buy a thousand boxes of canned goods from six different firms, and, with the view of perpetuating their own name, they put their own labels upon them. Some of these goods are sent to one province, some to another and some are exported out of the country altogether. I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture if it would be possible for his department to trace these goods to the manufacturer when there is no manufacturer's label upon the goods? Neither the wholesaler nor the department would be able to trace these goods.
Why not ?
Would the hon. gentleman state how ?

The amendment provides that :
Such dealer shall, upon request of the inspector, disclose the name of the packer of such article.

My hon. friend states that, but, at the same time, the special guarantor is the wholesale dealer. He is allowing the wholesale dealer to take the place of the manufacturer and I think this is dangerous legislation.

In reference to the purchase of the pack of a small packer that arises in this way : Those' who start canning factories in a small way are not usually people of capital. A number of those wishing to engage in the business come together and the first thing they do is to sell their pack. They must realize money on their first year's operations. They go to some large packer and make an arrangement with him by which he takes all their pack for that year Until they do that the bank will not advance one dollar to establish their business. Under the 12th section of the Act packages are required to be marked with the name of the packer and it is desired here to add :
Or of the first dealer obtaining it direct from the packer who sells or offers the same for sale.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman who has proposed this amendment, how he thinks it is going to work out practically. How is it going to operate in the ordinary course of trade ? I think I can tell him how it will operate. The wholesaler will say to

the packer : I will take your pack for this season, or some specified part of it, but I will insist upon putting my name upon the label. The packer naturally does not desire it. He has worked up a large value in his label during the course of many years' business. That is the proposition which is made to him by the wholesaler and the wholesalers combine to enforce that condition in all their purchases. They will all insist upon putting their own label on the goods and not the label of the packer.

The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Macpherson) said, in answer to my question as to how it was possible to trace the goods back to the manufacturer, that the packer would be compelled to put his name on the goods.
No, I did not say that.

The Act as it now stands says that:
_ All articles prepared for food in any establishment and packed in cans or similar receptacles, or in any package whatever, shall be subject to inspection during the whole course of preparation and packing ; and all such packages shall be marked with-
(a) the initials or the Christian names, the full surname, and the address, or, in the case of a firm or corporation, the firm or corporate name and address, of the packer.
And the amendment proposes to add :
Or of the first dealer obtaining it direct from the packer

Read on further.
Mr. ALCORN

-who sells or offers the same for sale.
Then go on.

The question then was as to how the packer could be traced and in answer to that the hon. member for Vancouver cited this part :
Such dealer shall, upon request of the inspector, disclose the name of the packer of such article.
But the packer's name need not be on the package at all.
That is quite true.

In the course of commercial dealing what will result from such legislation as this ? The result of this legislation will be to enable the wholesaler to put such pressure upon the packer as will compel the packer to allow his goods to go out altogether under the name of the wholesaler and thus entirely destroy the value of the label which the packer has established. The wholesaler can say : If you will not sell to me, or if your whole district will not
sell to me, I will get some one else to put up a factory ; a few of us will combine together, put up a factory and wipe you out of the business altogether.
For twenty years or over we have been operating in this way proposed by this amendment.
You are talking altogether of fish and we are talking altogether of fruit and vegetables.

My hon. friend cannot see anything outside of fruit and vegetables. But, my particular point is that we have been operating in this particular way for years. The hon. gentleman suggests as a reason why I bring in this amendment that the wholesalers would have the privilege of combining and forcing down prices. The reason is not that, and no argument that I have used can be construed by any hon gentleman to mean that. The hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Marshall) knows that I do not mean that and I take it that he is an authority upon these matters
Mr ALCORN Will the hon gentleman restrict his amendment to fish and fish products ?

There is no reason in the world why there should be any specific line of demarcation between these two classes of goods that I can see. I do not know but that there are many wholesalers operating in connection with fruit and vegetables as well ; I cannot say that.

Would it answer the purpose if you changed the amendment iu such a way as to provide that after the word 'packer' the following words be added: ' And any subsequent dealer who sells or offers the same for sale must add thereto his own brand or mark ' ?
No, that would be making my amendment nugatory.

It would not make it nugatory. The strongest point of the observations which have been made seems to be that if any good will had been created in the trade mark of a wholesale dealer or exporter it would be desirable, if possible, to preserve that and, at the same time, pre serve the general principle of the Act by keeping the name of the packer upon the can. There are some cases in which the name of the nfan, who is not, strictly speaking, the packer, may properly be upon the can. I know that in Nova Scotia, for example, a man who deals in lobsters, sometimes has not his own factory at ail. He has lobsters packed according to a .certain specification which is carefully written out and embodied in the terms of a contract. He has the canning of these lobsters

inspected by men appointed by himself, so that, in effect, they are really canned under his own supervision although not canned actually in his own factory. Then his own label is supplied to the persons whom he so employs and it is put upon the goods. But, the amendment which is suggested does not apply to that ease at all. It is the case in which a wholesale dealer buys up a pack which perhaps he has not examined at all. I think it is highly desirable to preserve the principle of the Act and have the packer's name on the can, and at the same time preserve the good will which has inured in that way to a wholesaler by having his name on the package as well. It seems to me that the two ideas could be worked out together.

I really cannot follow my hon. frend through that because that would result in the goods of a man who had made his label -well known being obliged to carry two different names. I do not think that would be fair. My hon. friend makes a mistake in saying that the wholesaler does not inspect his fish.

I gathered that
sometimes he did not inspect.
He would not jeopardize the good name of his firm by putting his label on a poor pack.
How is it possible to trace the goods to the canner?

My amendment
says :
Such dealer shall, upon the request of an inspector appointed under this Act, disclose the name of the packer of such goods.

Suppose James Turner & Co., of Hamilton, buy 1,000 boxes from six different canning companies and they are all labelled under the name of James Turner & Co., how would it be possible to trace the packer after the goods are distributed throughout Canada?
I should not think there would be any difficulty. James Turner & Co.'s name is on the tin and the in-pector would go to that firm and ask from whom they bought.
How would they know which of the six different establishments that tin came from?
He will he obliged under this Act to keep track.
What objection can there be to compelling the canner as well as the wholesaler to put his name on the label?

The wholesaler as a rule will buy the output of a factory, and it Mr. R. J- BORDEN.
is the easiest thing in the world to keep track.

But suppose James Turner & Co. buy part of their stock from the Canadian canners and part from the Homestead and the goods are distributed and three months afterwards claims are made, how can a distinction be drawn between the.goods?
James Turner & Co. will be held responsible.

Yes, but the claims all come back to the canner, and it is impossible to tell which canner the claim should come to unless his name Is on the label. If a firm bought from one company it could be done, but where they buy from different companies it cannot be done.

To show the outrageous character of this proposition, it is merely sufficient to mention that the responsibility for making good faulty goods is on the packer ; he is the man who is to be made to pay in case anything goes wrong, but the proposition is to give the whole value in the label to the wholesale dealer. The packer's label is wiped out, but the packer must pay all the losses in the end.
I would like the minister to answer the question as to whether under this proposal it would be possible for the consumer of the article to trace the manufacturer of the article?

That is a matter of opinion. I gather from what my hon. friend from Elgin said that in the past they have been able to do that when the packer's name was not on the label, and if that be so they ought to be able to do it in the future. I say that if they were able to trace the packers in the past before this Act came into force, they ought to be able to do it in the future. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) spoke about my duty in the matter. My duty is to try and see that this Act safeguards the public interest, and I thought it did so, but when I examined the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Macpherson) I thought it provided a sufficient guarantee for the public interest and having that belief, although I did not propose the amendment, I did not see any objection to its adoption if the committee wished to adopt it. It was not in the original Act, and were it not for the representations of the wholesale trade generally of Canada-I think I may say from the Atlantic to the Pacific-I would not have known there was any objection to the original Act. It seems to me that there is a perfect safeguard for the public whether the amedment Is passed or not. and that being so it does not matter to me very much personally whether the amendment passes or does not pass. The other night the committee approved of the amendment.

I said then, as may be found in ' Hansard,' that I did not see any objection to it in the public interest, and as the committee has adopted it I would prefer it to remain and shall vote, if it comes to a vote, to sustain the opinion of the committee. I wish to say a word to my hon. friend from Bast Elgin (Mr. Marshall). He has stated that the Canadian canners purchased canned goods from other canners and put their label on them, and in my opinion that gives away his case. He may not agree with me in that, but that is my view of it. It does not seem to me to make a bit of difference whether it is a canner or a wholesaler who puts his name on goods he does not himself pack. I grant that if the Canadian canners pack the goods themselves their names might be an additional guarantee over and above what the wholesaler who does not himself pack the goods could give. But if the Canadian canner buy from another canner goods which they themselves do not pack and put their mark on these goods they are doing the same as the wholesale grocer does when he buys his goods from another canner and puts his mark on them. 1 cannot see any difference. My hon. friend says that they are practical canners arid would inspect the goods. The wholesaler is just as well able to employ a practical canner to inspect the goods he buys as are the canners and is just as likely to do so. My hon. friend (Mr. Alcorn) said the difficulty was that the man who established a new cannery would be at the mercy of the wholesale trade. He said the new cannery could not sell its own goods because it was not known, and I understood him to mention that it would then sell to another cannery or packing house. I cannot see that that differs in any way from selling to a wholesaler, and I do not think that they are any more in the power of the wholesaler than of the old established cannery.
I gave that as the method by which these purchases are made, the trade reasons that arise why these goods are bought in that way. It is not an ordinary transaction.

I do not think it makes any difference whether the wholesale or another packing house buys from the small cannery. In both eases they are goods produced in the new cannery by beginners and the wholesaler puts on them his guarantee that he will be responsible for the quality of the goods. In another case an old established cannery puts its mark on. It seems to me that the guarantee of the wholesale house of the quality of the goods is no better and no worse than the guarantee of another canning house. The hon. member for Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) asked the hon. member for Hamilton about Crosse & Blackwell. He knows perfectly well that Crosse & Blackwell do not them-230
selves pack one-hundredth part or a one-thousandth part of the goods on which they put their name. They buy goods put up in Canada, have them sent to England and put the Crosse & Blackwell mark on them, and the Crosse & Blackwell mark carries them all over the world. Crosse & Blackwell are in England, a packing house, but as far as the trade of the world is concerned, they are a wholesale house and not a packing house. They buy fruits from British Columbia, California, Ontario, and Nova Scotia, vegetables from Ontario, they send them to England and put the Crosse & Blackwell mark on them and that mark carries them all over the world, just as a wholesale house in Hamilton, Montreal or Toronto might buy goods in different parts of Canada, put their name upon them, and in that way guarantee the quality of the goods. My hon. friend's reference to Crosse & Blackwell was rather unfortunate for his argument.
I am not going to argue one way or the other. I did not introduce this amendment because I did not know it was necessary. When it was brought forward by my hon. friend from Vancouver (Mr, Macpherson) and shown to be necessary in the interest of a very large class of the community, I examined it to see whether it was going in any way to injure the public interest. I found that to my mind it would not and therefore accepted it and agreed to it. Having accepted it, and agreed to it, and the committee having accepted and agreed to it, I confess that no argument has been advanced why it should not be accepted and if it comes to a vote I shall have to vote for the retention of the amendment.
When the Bill was first introduced was its object not to improve the quality of the canned goods of the country ?
Yes.
To my mind you have taken the back-bone out of your Act.

I cannot see that. If I thought that I would not support it.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I desire to ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) a question. Section 12 provides that articles prepared for food and packed shall be marked in certain ways. Subsection (b) provides that such goods shall be marked with
(b) a true and correct description of the contents of the package:
Provided, however, that if it be established to the satisfaction of the Governor in Council that such marking would hinder the



sale of any said articles in the British or foreign markets he may exempt such articles from the provisions of this section.
Have any regulations been made with respect to canned lobsters or other fish under subsection b of section 12?
No.

I would like to explain that, in the maritime provinces, and especially in the province of Prince Edward Island there are several men who buy canned lobsters from the packers.
