They instruct the packers how to put up these lobsters, the work being done according to formulae furnished by the buyers in Europe, especially in France. The goods are labelled with the brand of the man who buys from the packer. I do not think it would be advisable to change that method of doing business.
I would like to ask the bon. gentleman a question. Do I understand him to say that in England they require that the cans shall be sent there without labels?

I do not know that. But I know that the practice in the maritime provinces and especially in Prince Edward Island is as I have described it. And these men who buy from the packers have established a trade. The goods are put up under the inspection of these men. I think it would be unfair to change their methods of busiuess. I would agree with the hon. member for Vancouver city (Mr. Macpherson) so far as the packing of fish is concerned. It may be that a different method should be followed with respect to fruits. But I have some knowledge of the fish packing business, and, so far as that is concerned, I would agree with the amendment proposed.
Mr. ,T. D. REID. I was not here during the earlier part of this discussion. But, as I understand, the amendment makes it unnecessary to have the name of the original packer on the can.
The packer or the first dealer.

Under this amendment the wholesaler can write to the packer telling him to put up so many cans and label them, ' Packed for such a wholesale firm.' And the name of the original packer does not appear. But, is the wholesale man held entirely responsible for the quality of the goods? Would he be liable to prosecution if the goods were not as required by law?
Yes.
With the additional safeguard that, if required, the wholesaler must disclose the name of the packer.

But whom would you prosecute in a ease of that kind? There was a case in Montreal last year where some 50,000 cans, of salmon I think it was, led to a good deal of trouble. I think some people were poisoned, or at least made ill, by eating the stuff. In that case they could not find out-
There was no name on those packages at all.
I did not understand that. But, under this amendment, as I understand it, it would be impossible to put out canned goods without the name of some responsible party on the packages.
Absolutely.

It appears to me that we are attempting to legislate in the same terms on two very different subjects. It is apparent from what has been said by the hon. member from Vancouver City and by the hon. members from the maritime provinces tnat the course of business with regard to the sale of fish and fish products differs materially from that followed in Ontario with regard to vegetables and fruit. I do not think it possible to frame a section which will be satisfactorily applicable to both these kinds of business. Therefore, I move, seconded by Mr. Marshall, that the amendment be amended by inserting after the word ' or ' the words ' (in the case of fish and fish products).'

I think the position is not quite understood. The change made at the instance of the hon. member for Vancouver City (Mr. Macpherson) is not an amendment, but is a part of the Bill. Therefore, this is not an amendment to the amendment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understand that the Bill is referred back for the purpose of considering an amendment.
But the clause moved as an amendment is part of the Bill as printed. It was adopted in committee and is a part of the Bill as it stood for third reading.

But the fact that we are considering that clause is proof that it was not passed. The order was to go back into committee to consider that clause.
Mr. F'ISHER. Yes, clause, but not amendment.
But it is not finally decided until the clause is passed.

The government is doing the packer a great injustice. These men have been building up a trade and a reputation for years, and now they are denied the privilege of placing their own name upon their goods.
Not at all.

If the wholesale man refuses to buy these goods with the packer's name on them, it virtually amounts to the same thing. When people go to buy those goods and ask for a certain man's brand of canned goods, they have got to take the dealer's word for it.
The hon. gentleman has not read the Bill.

Canadian canners are willing to put up their goods with the wholesale grocer's name on them, but they also want to put their own name on them. According to this Bill any wholesale manufacturer, or some men that are not particular as to the quality of goods, will put up inferior goods, though they may possibly pass the law ; yet they put on the wholesale grocer's name, and the goods can be sold to the injury of the reputation of Canadian goods as a whole. I can't see any reason why the law should not allow the actual packer's name to be placed on the goods so that they, can be followed up to their origin. If you went into a retail store and purchased canned goods with simply the wholesale dealer's name on them, you do not know who put up the goods.
The hon. gentleman has not read the Bill, or he would not make a statement like that.

In the ' Globe ' of April 8, I find an item which bears out my contention. It reads as follows :
Winnipeg, April 7.
The health authorities have seized 330 cases, each containing six one-gallon cans of apples, and they are on the watch for six more cases in the same consignment, of which there is at present no trace. The goods are declared by the health officers to be absolutely unfit for food. All bore the label of an Oshawa Canning Company. Prosecution will follow.
In that case you can trace the name of the manufacturer, and you are able to prosecute him, and you are able to show the public the company that is not putting up a good article.

The hon. gentleman as a business man will understand this proposition. A wholesale firm has been purchasing the output of a canning factory, they have established a reputation and have a label for a certain class of canned salmon. No other names ever appear on these cans except the name of that firm. The wholesale firm may have bought this salmon from a different factory every year, for the reason that one factory or another may have met with a failure. Wholesale traders in British Columbia who went out and bought 4,000 or 5,000 cases of salmon and put their own label on it and sent it to the markets of the world, obliged to buy 2304
from two or three different factories, have found themselves in the position of putting up this year canned salmon with John Jones' name on it ; next year James Smith's name would be on it, and in a very short time the reputation of their goods would be gone. People will say, this is not the same thing, because this label never carried these goods before. The merchants in British Columbia have found themselves badly handicapped by the operation of the present Act. My good friend from Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) brings in the question of fish. Now we have small canneries who put up both fruit and fish. I do not know whether they are putting labels on their cans or not, but the wholesale houses are buying them. This amendment protects the public, and it does not place the wholesale merchants or canners in any worse position than they have been in for many years.

Take the case of fish. They might put up a can of fish that was taken from different parts of the country, and all might not be of the same quality. The effect of the wholesale man putting his name on it would be a guarantee to the public, because the public would know who produced those goods and where they were produced. The particular locality the fish comes from is what the public would like to know. I really think that the wholesale man should not object to the manufacturer's name going on so that he can show the public where these goods are made,, and in case they are not good you can go on and prosecute the manufacturer. The very fact of the name of the manufacturer and the words ' made in Canada ' being on these labels is evidence to the public that the goods are of the proper quality. I could mention cases where the dealer goes to some other country and gets goods put up simply because they are a little cheaper although they are not of the same quality as our own canned goods. It should be the duty of the government to protect our own manufacturers and -wholesale men and no wholesale man in Canada to-day will, if he has the interest of the country at heart, object to the name of any Canadian manufacturer being placed on these labels. I quite understand, as the hon. member for Vancouver has said, that in British Columbia the wholesale men are using these special labels. One wholesale man will get a name for his goods, another will get another name for his goods and yet they are all manufactured in the same factory. In a case such as the hon. member mentions, where it is absolutely necessary the public should be protected, I cannot see why they should object to the name of the manufacturer being on the label as has been the practice in times past.

The hon. member for Leeds has classed the wholesale Grocers' Association of Canada as being composed

of people who do not care for the interests of the trade in Canada.
I do not think so.
That is what the hon. gentleman said.
I did not know that I did.
No, the hon. gentleman did not know, but he spoke of the people asking for this amendment in that way and the people who are asking for this amendment are the wholesale trade of the country.

I think that both sides of the House want to arrive at some result beneficial to the manufacturers and consumers. If goods are manufactured by so and so for so and so and if you find that these goods are wrong how are you going to trace them up and find out where the trouble is ? We have heard of several cases of goods being sent out which have poisoned people and if the name of the manufacturer is not on the goods how are you going to trace them back ?
Has my hon. friend read the Act ?
Part of it.
Well, let him read the whole of it and perhaps he will not say that.

If the minister states the wholesale men are the ones which are making application for this change then I say they are looking after their own interests more than they are looking after the interests of the people as a whole. Suppose some irresponsible person goes to a manufacturer and asks him to put up 500 cases of an inferior quality of goods and this person, after disposing of these goods leaves the country, there is no way of prosecuting because there is no person to hold responsible. If the manufacturer's name is on the goods you can prosecute him but you cannot hold accountable an irresponsible commission man.

Would it not be as possible for a canner who had no more appreciation of his duties then a commission man to do the same thing ? The fact of the matter is that wholesale firms have been operating for years with these special labels ; under the present Act the canners have to have their names on the packages. The wholesale men are to all intents and purposes the manufacturers. They go to the factory and say : I am prepared to buy
5,000	cases of salmon but I want them to be put under my brand. That brand protects the wholesaler in the market.
How would the hon. gentleman do in the case that I have mentioned ?
I would put the man in jail, of course.

But you could not get him.
Mr. MACPHERSON1. You cannot save people from being bad.
Could you not if the manufacturer's name was on the label ?

No, you could not any more than you could in the other case. If my hon. friend's imagination shows him how wicked a commission merchant might be he can also imagine how wicked the small canner might be. I know of a small canner who packed Cohoes fish that were too long out of the water and he could not get anybody to take them off his hands.

I feel very much disposed to vote against all these amendments. I think there is too much law, a great deal too much law and while I am not so dense, and while I have been listening to this discussion the whole afternoon, I think I know less about it now than I did when it commenced. I have no doubt that it will appeal to the public in the same way. There is too much law on the statute-book and there is not enough to carry out the purpose that the framer of the law has had in his mind. We have heard about the rotten fish that was offered for sale last year iu Montreal and although the sale of that fish did a lot of harm nothing could be done. There was no law to deal with the case. Although we have the statute-books filled up with laws we have not enough law to provide for a case of that kind. The consumer has been entirely forgotten in this discussion. It is a mere fight between the packers and the jobbers and the whole of the time has been taken for the last four or five hours in an effort to see who can make the most out of it-the packers or the jobbers. That is not the object that the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) had in his mind, I am sure, when he undertook, in the first instance, to protect the public against the adulteration of food. The hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Mac-pherson) has nothing else in his mind or in view but fish. The object of his amendment is entirely different from the purpose of my hon. friends behind me who are interested in the packing of tomatoes, peas and other vegetables. I understand the position of my hon. friend from Vancouver, but, of course, we cannot legislate only for him or for those engaged in the fish trade. The position taken by my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. A. A. Me-

Lean) is the same as that of the hon. member for Vancouver. In their case the commercial men take the fish of certain packers. The packers are the secondary persons, they do not conduct the trade, but they are the employees of the men who do carry on the trade in fish. The merchants engage five or ten packers to pack fish for them and they require them to pack fish in different ways to suit different markets. A lobster dealer will go to a packer and say : I want you to pack lobsters In such and such a way for the German market and he will say to another packer : I want you to pack fish in such and such a way for the French trade. In that case the packer disappears completely. The commercial men are the ones who look after this trade. Those are the men that my hon. friend had In his eye when he moved this amendment. But, the position taken by my hon. friend from East Elgin (Mr. Marshall) is entirely different. He and other packers have created something. They can peas or tomatoes and they want to do it in such a perfect way that they will drive from the Canadian market all foreign produce of that kind. It was stated in a very open way that Americans come here and sell an article for 25 cents a package when our friends can put up two packages of the same kind of goods for a quarter. Still the American article takes the lead because of the name or for some other reason. The two interests represented are entirely different and we have lost the whole afternoon in a fight between the packers and jobbers. I appeal again to the Minister of Agriculture. We want to keep the consumer in our eye. He is the one that we are legislating for. We do not want to harm the packers or the jobbers, but they can take care of themselves. It is the consumer we have to take care of. The Minister of Agriculture should insert a clause providing that an inspector could enter a cannery and ascertain whether the goods were in proper condition or not. For my part I would like to see a government stamp on all these canned goods so that the consumer would have ample security that he is protected. After all it is the interests of the consumer that we should look after primarily in this matter.

I cannot understand why the minister compels shippers to put their name on the fruit which is the raw material of these canneries, and deny to the manufacturer the privilege of putting his name on the manufactured article. The Minister of Agriculture compels the shipper of apples to place his name on every barrel that leaves this country so that if there is any fraud in the packing the shipper may be traced, but at the same time the minister takes away from the public
the privilege of buying any brand of canned goods they desire to buy from the retailers.
Where does the hon. gentleman get that in the Act ?
There is nothing on the label to show who manufactured the goods.

The hon. member for Vancouver has been arguing all afternoon w ith regard to the trade of his province in fish and the amendment prepared by me gives him all he asks for, but yet he is not disposed to accept it. That is evidence to my mind of what I suspected all along, that this is a determined effort on the part of the wholesalers to compel the canners to sell to them and give them control of the trade.

If the government would accept fish from the provisions of this Act, that is all the fish packers of the maritime provinces and British Columbia have asked, and if the minister gives an undertaking that that will be bone, these useless amendments might be dropped.

There is nothing useless about the amendment because the wholesale grocers have been operating under it for the last eight months, and I think the trade have a pretty fair appreciation of what they want.
If this Act passes in its present shape the public will certainly not be able to tell who packs the goods.

It would appear that the wholesale grocers are the only ones interested in this Bill. It seems that this Bill Is not in the interests of the canners or the public and that it is passed only to please the wholesale grocers.

I would ask the Minister of Agriculture, if this Bill passes, can a wholesale merchant in Toronto import from the Fnited States canned goods which have not the name of the packer, and by putting his own name on them sell them to the people of Canada ?

The Bill applies to all goods sold in Canada and the importer would be responsible for the quality of the goods. Under the Act of last session the packer in the United States would be responsible for the quality of the goods and nobody in Canada would be responsible. The amendment proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. Macpherson) does not prevent any packer insisting that his name should be on the package ; that is a trade arrangement between him and the wholesaler. This Bill simply provides that the first dealer purchasing from the packer may put his label on instead of that of the original packer, but if an inspector desires

it he must divulge the name of the original packer. If I thought this amendment lessened the protection for the public in any way I would not have accepted it the other night, and believing that the public is amply protected I am not prepared to-day to vote down what the House agreed to the other day. It appears to be largely a quarrel between the packers on the one hand and the wholesalers on the other and I am not prepared to judge between them.
It is not a quarrel between the canner and the wholesaler at all.
I cannot see that the guarantee of one is not just as good as the guarantee of the other.

It is not as good a guarantee to the consumer. My object is to protect the interests of the consumer. I believe that a packer who does not put his name on the label would not be so careful as he would if he knew the goods were going out under his name. These special labels which state that the goods are put up by so and so for the wholesale buyer have been used for some time and I do not see why you want to change that.

If the wholesaler says to the packer: I will only buy your goods on condition that you do not put on your name, then the packer has to comply with that or lose the trade An American citizen can send in here an inferior quality of canned goods, distribute them under the name of some person in Canada which may bo fictitious and if anything is found wrong he can move across the other side of the line. The minister has been met by a deputation of wholesale grocers and he seems to have nothing else in his mind but to protect their interests. The very fact that there were 50,000 cases of canned fish in the city of Montreal poisoning the people last fall should be sufficient to convince the Minister of Agriculture that the consumers of Canada need protection. I would suggest that the minister take this matter into further consideration and hear representations from manufacturers. the wholesale men, and some one on behalf of the public. He should prepare a Bill that would- protect all and be in the interests of Canada as a whole. The Senate will not meet for two or three weeks; he has plenty of time and there is no object in putting the Bill through tonight. For that reason I ask that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.

I cannot understand why the minister is so anxious, in the case of the Fruit Marks Act for instance, the person who packs apples must put his stamp on the package, while he does not insist on that in t^is case. As has been pointed out, this is Mr. FISHER.
only class legislation in the interest of the wholesale dealer.
Nothing of the kind.

The minister pointed out last year that the change would place the responsibility on the wholesale man. In order that his memory may be refreshed, I shall read what he then said at page 6773 of ' Hansard
I think all necessary safeguards can be thrown about the Bill with this additional amendment; and, as I have wished all through to interfere as little as possible with the course of trade, I have asked the House to add these words, which would enable the dealer, or the packer who was having goods packed for him outside of his own packing house, to put his name upon them and be responsible for them instead of the actual packer.
There is no doubt that this is class legislation for some particular purpose which I cannot understand. In my opinion this will permit the dealers in western Canada to import canned goods from the United States without a name upon them, place their own names on and sell them. On December 10, last, a return was ordered:
Showing what complaints respecting the inadequacy of postal service or delays therein, or respecting lack of or defects in postal facilities or means of communications, have been received by the Post Office Department since the 1st day of January, 1907, and the general nature of such complaints.
I thought that was a reasonable request to make of the Postmaster General, but it is now nearly five months since the order for that return was passed. I was assured some months ago that the Postmaster General was preparing the return, but that it took a good deal of time and care. Consequently, they were not able to bring it down any sooner. However, I cannot but think that, if that is the case, the Post Office Department is not in a very flourishing condition and is not the model department, one would suppose it to be, from the remarks we have heard made concerning it. I can only say that I have received a
number of most damaging communications in referrence to the affairs of that department and the irregularities therein. I am anxious to get the information that will come down in the return, that I may see whether these matters have been straightened out to the satisfaction of the public.
Another matter I would like the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) to consider is with regard to the weekly papers. On several occasions I have called his attention to the serious position of the weekly papers in Canada. I understand that the Postmaster General has placed a man in the United States to take charge of papers addressed to people in the United States and distribute them. The publishers are at the expense, inconvenience and delay of that system. The Postmaster General, in reply to questions I asked him in regard to these matters, made the following statement on April 9 :
I received this morning a communication from the Weekly Section of the Canadian Press Association, and they are perfectly satisfied with the answer given.
Well, Sir, I have here communications from a large number of the weekly papers in different parts of Canada, not one in favour of the arrangement that the Postmaster General has now made for handling these papers, but every one condemning in the strongest language this action of the government, not only with regard to weekly papers, but with regard to the daily papers also. Now, the Postmaster General must admit that on the 8th of May last, when he brought in this regulation dealing with the daily and weekly papers, he was placing those papers in a very unfair position. He has been forced to back down from the position he took last May and to restore the daily papers to the position in which they were previous to that time. He has also been compelled to pay tens of thousands of dollars of the people's money out of the public chest to satisfy them in a reasonable way for the loss they have suffered. I would like the Postmaster General to explain the difference in the position of the country to-day as compared with that in which it was in May last in regard to these papers. He will tell us, perhaps, as he has told us on previous occasions, that he has been able to stop at the border all the literature that is of a character that we should not like to have enter our country. If that is the case, what legislation has he placed on the statute-book or why has he gone back on the position with regard to the daily papers which he occupied previous to last year? There is no doubt that the Postmaster General had as good a right then to stop daily or weekly papers of an undesirable character from coming into the country as he has now. There can be no doubt that if he . will (appoint censors to deal with these

papers, he has power to stop objectionable matter from coming into Canada. At page 3266 of * Hansard ' of this year it will be seen that he said :
So, we are perfectly free to accept or to reject any periodicals, bnt the House and the country may feel assured that we shall accept only the good periodicals.
He has had to back down from his position in regard to the daily papers, and he is gradually backing down in regard to the weekly papers. What I would like him to do is to come out boldly and manfully and say that he has made a blunder and is will' ing to take it back; that he is willing to remedy the existing state of affairs and give the newspapers reasonable compensation for the loss they have suffered.
Now, will the Postmaster General please answer me with regard to another matter -and I will ask him to take note of these points and reply to them as best he thinks. I notice that in reply to some questions I asked during the present session in connection with the purchase of a steamer in Great Britain by the Post Office Department, it appeared that the government had seen fit to pay $60,000 for the steamer and $3,500 for bringing her over.
What is she employed for ?

Carrying the mail from the Transatlantic steamers at Rimou-ski. The steamer carries twenty-two men. So besides the cost of the steamer and of bringing her to this side, it will cost in the neighbourhood of $20,000 or $30,000 a year to run her. And the business that she is to do was being carried out under contract with a private firm for about $4,000 per annum. Will the minister explain in what way this is good business? I understand on very good authority that the new boat is so large and cumbersome that the large liners have expressed a wish that she should not be sent out during rough weather to take the mails, but that the smaller tender be sent out during storms. I might also say that reports are current that when the boat came over in May last
What is the name of the boat?

The ' Lady Evelyn.' It is stated that though she came in May last she was not used for carrying the mails until the 20th of August and she made twenty-four round trips. But during this time the contract under which this work was to be done for $4,000 a year was still in force. The minister might explain this. Another thing is this :	It is reported that the minister and quite a gathering of friends went for a trip in this boat and spent a good deal of time and a great deal of the people's money in cruising about. I cannot say that I have any definite knowledge of that mat-

ter, but these are the reports that come in and I think it but right that the minister should have an opportunity of explaining them away.
There is still another question I would like the minister to deal with. According to his own reports, last year he paid the railways in the neighbourhood of $1,600,000. I have no definite knowledge about the manner in which that money is expended. We know that in the United States the mail is weighed. We know also that a representative in the United States legislature made the statement in his place that over $70,000,000 of the people's money had been wasted owing to the false weighing of the mails by the railways. The minister in reply to a question I asked stated, as I understood him, that the mails in Canada were not weighed, but that they were paid for according to some arrangement with the railways. I think it would be interesting to the country to know just in what manner the mails are carried so far as the railways are concerned.
Another matter with respect to which I would like information is the one-cent drop letter that he promised the people in the cities some months ago, possibly a year ago. People are anxiously waiting for him to reply as to the position he is going to take. I would like him to tell the House in what position he is going to place the smaller towns aud rural districts in regard to a cheaper mail service, and what advantage he is going to give them as an offset to the advantages he is giving the cities. The cities are receiving important benefits at the present time in the way of mail delivery, and a great deal of money is being expended upon them, and we who live in rural districts naturally feel that sufficient attention is not being given to us in the way of affording corresponding better mail facilities. The minister says that he is only giving free delivery to towns with a population of 12,000 and a revenue of $20,000. But if he will look across the line into the United States he will see that free delivery is given to cities with 10,000 inhabitants and a revenue of $10,000. The minister seems to be surprised at that, but if he will look into the matter he will find that is the case. He will also find that the Postmaster General of the United States has made several successful experiments in giving free delivery to towns with a population as low as 2,500.
I think the minister should be able to give us a better explanation than he did to-day when, in reply to a question of one of the Toronto members, he told us that the matter was under consideration. The minister has,
I think, a surplus of a million and a half dollars this year. What is he going to do with it? Is he going to let it pass into other departments to be squandered in the same way as they have been squandering the people's money the last few years ? Is it unreasonable for the rural districts to ask

for a better mail service? If you look around this House you will find that out of 214 members there are possibly 14 representing purely city constituencies, while the other 200 represent, either entirely rural districts or districts partially rural and partially urban. The minister is now considering a proposition to grant to cities a one-cent drop letter system; let him at the same time consider some way of improving the mail service in the rural districts.
I would like him also to give the House some definite statement of his intention with regard to free rural mail delivery. He may think that is a matter of trifling importance, but if he will look around this country he will find that it is a question of vital importance to large numbers of people. Last year he told us that this proposition was a luxury, it could only be looked upon as an ideal, and he said that we might have to wait till this country had a population of
20,000,000. For my part I think the time is already ripe for the Postmaster General to put into effect this important legislation. I will not go into the question fully to-night, because I have already dealt with it at an earlier period of the session. But the more I investigate the matter the more convinced I feel that this is a reform that should be adopted at the earliest possible moment.
The hon. gentleman advocates rural free mail delivery. I would like to know whether he advocates such delivery over the whole of Canada, or only a Part, and if only a part, what part.

The hon. gentleman has asked a question that he would not have asked if he had investigated this subject thoroughly. I have never advocated the establishment of rural free mail delivery over the whole of Canada. I have explained clearly that wherever this system has been established, whether in the United States, or England, or Germany, or Switzerland, or France, it has been established under strict regulations that are found to be satisfactory. In the United States the president has established a commission of three men to deal with this question, not more than two of whom must be of the same political party. On that commission there are two Republicans, and one of the most prominent Democrats in the United States, Mr. Black. These men have full power to deal with this question, and when they appoint officials in any branch of the service, party politics are completely ignored by them. One of the regulations in the United States is that the route must be 24 miles long, and there must be 100 families living on that route, out of whom 85 at least must be prepared to place a box at their gate where the mail can be deposited. That rule is strictly enforced. If the route is short and the expense of carriage is less, the number of families to be served may be less.

The hon. gentleman stated that the selection of routes was left entirely to an independent commission. Is he aware that in a periodical known as the ' Postmaster's Journal,' printed in the United States, the November number of last year states explicitly that the mail routes are made up largely for the benefit of the representatives, and not for the benefit of the people?
I do not believ.e that the hon. gentleman can furnish any facts whatever that would bear out his statement.
I can furnish the hon. gentleman with the statement in this journal.

The hon. gentleman will not find on investigation that politics enter into the administration of this service at all. The most enthusiastic advocate of the reform is the president himself. The editor of the ' Canadian Dairyman ' has been over to the United States and made a thorough investigation, and in his paper for the last two weeks he has stated that mere is no such thing as politics in the management of the rural free mail delivery system in the United States. I have been over there myself and investigated the question.

The hon. gentleman must admit that he can get only a superficial knowledge of the influence of polities in the administration of that system, by merely going over to the United States and visiting the departmental buildings.

I have been in the habit of visiting the United States more or less for the last fifteen years or twenty years, and my investigations have convinced me that what the hon. gentleman says is an error. Now, I do not wish to deal any further with this than to say that five-sixths of the territory of the United States is practically covered to-day and that 20.000,000 people in the rural districts enjoy the privilege of rural free mail delivery. ' While, in 1897. when rural free mail delivery was first established, the deficit in the United States postal department was over $11,000,000, when the expenditure for rural free mail delivery was $14,000, last year, while the expenditure was in the neighbourhood of $30,000,000. the deficit was only a little over $6,000,000 and the Postmaster General himself has distinctly stated that for the first four months of this year there was no deficit at all and that as far as the rural free mail delivery end of it is concerned instead of it being a deficit producer it is a revenue producer. I am satisfied that the Postmaster General will not get up to-night and make the statements in regard to the expenditures and deficits that lie made last year and that the Minister of

Agriculture will not repeat the words that he used in Quebec when he told the people how this question staggered him and how he did not even advise the discussion of it in the House. These are the questions that I want to put before the Postmaster General. I did not know of any other way of bringing them to the attention of the House .and the country and I am sure the Postmaster General will be good enough to reply to me.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad that my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) has called the attention of the House to some matters concerning the Post Office Department. The department is so well administered apparently that I have not heard much criticism about it for a few weeks, although my hon. friend is the official critic of that department. I will be pleased to answer the questions which have been so graciously put by my hon. friend to-night on the different subjects which, he says, have attracted his attention for the last few months. First of all he is anxious to obtain information as regards the return concerning the irregularities reported in the Post Office Department during the last year. This return was moved for by the hon. gentleman during my absence in Japan at the beginning of the session. I have, on two occasions, informed my hon. friend that the officers of the department were anxious to prepare the return as soon as possible ; in fact out of ten or twelve returns which were moved for by hon. members on the other side of the House this year in the Post Office Department all have been laid on the table of the House with the solitary exception of my hon. friend's return. But, my hon. friend will admit that this return entails a good deal of work and, while there are very few irregularities, the officers have to look into every pigeon hole of the department to ascertain what few irregularities were reported during the year and as my hon. friend knows this takes a good deal of time and involves a good deal of work. I am as anxious to lay on the table of the House a list of these irregularities as my hon. friend is to have it. He will see, in looking over the return, when it is laid on the table, that with the millions of letters, packages ;and parcel packages passing through His Majesty's mails in Canada there are very [DOT]few 'irregularities and the department is very soon informed of any such irregularities that occur in any section of the country. My hon. friend is entitled to the return and I can assure him that he will get it as soon as possible. The officers of the department, notwithstanding that they are overtaxed during the session, are only too willing to gratify the demand made by the hon. member.
My hon. friend has called my attention to the weekly papers. I need not repeat what I have already stated to the Mr. ARMSTRONG.
House on a former occasion. I know that there is some agitation in some parts of the country concerning weekly papers. You are aware, Mr. Speaker, that last year, on account of circumstances which I have fully explained, we had to amend our postal convention with the Washington authorities. That amendment was directed wholly against certain classes of periodicals published in the United States and Canada up to that date obliged both countries to carry according to their respective domestic rates, periodicals and newspapers coming under what, in the postal service, is called second class matter. I have explained on many occasions to the House where the difficulty was as it affected Canada. With the increase in the number of periodicals published in the United States and with the' enormons increase in the number of purely advertising sheets published on the other side of the line we had to put our whole mail service at the disposal of United States publishers. Besides, we had received for years, complaints from clergymen of the different denominations, against certain undesirable papers which were circulated through our mails in Canada. We thought that wre should revise our postal convention with the United States, so as to protect not only ourselves but even the United States, as we were told by the American postal authorities last year. To clear ourselves of that class of literature, the postal rate on second class matter was raised from one to four cents a pound; that is to say, papers mailed in Canada for the United States have to pay at the rate of 4 cents per pound. It is the same with papers posted. in the United States. My hon. friend was asking a minute ago what legislation had been introduced to purge our mails from undesirable literature. Let me tell my hon. friend at once that I claim -and I claim the credit not only for myself but for the officers of the department-* that we have nearly purged the Canadian mails of undesirable literature and I am sure that is a fact which will be welcomed by both sides of the House.
Will the minister be good enough to tell us just what he did that made such a radical change ; what legislation or regulation did he introduce ?

Nothing appears on the statute-book because we have a postal convention with the United States. It is in that convention and not in the statute-book that my hon. friend will find the remedy. Under that convention, undesirable periodicals coming from the United States have to pay not one but four cents a pound. There is nothing as effective as a high postal rate to check the importation of undesirable literature.

What about the great family journal, the Calgary ' Eye-Opener '- ever see that ?

- Mr. LEMIEUX. I do not read undesirable literature ; my bon. friend (Mr. Bennett), perhaps, does. If he does I am sorry and I hope he will not do it again.
It is your loss.
As far as daily papers are concerned they are placed back just where they were, as I understand it.
No, I will answer my hon. friend.
And as far as weeklies are concerned

I was just coming to them, if my hon. friend will allow me. I understand what he wants to know.. We have purged the mails of undesirable literature coming from the United States and besides, we have protected our commercial interests by preventing these purely advertising sheets from being dumped in our mail system. The hon. gentleman asks how it is we have rescinded the arrangement made last year with the Washington authorities as regards newspapers. Well, I had to take a radical step to begin with, but I did not intend to maintain that attitude towards the dailies. The hon. gentleman is a reader of the American press as I am. and he will agree with me that as a rule the American daily papers subscribed for by Canadians are respectable journals. Our rule was directed more against American dime novels and other unsavory periodicals. I maintained the rule against such objectionable periodicals and I gave the dailies a rate of one cent a pound. The editors of the weekly press, a very representative body, waited on me on the 9th April with the object of obtaining the same postal rate as the daily newspapers. I must say that the weekly press is favoured in some respects as compared with the daily press. A section of our postal guide reads :
A further exception is made in favour of newspapers or periodicals published not more frequently than once a week which may be sent free to regular subscribers in Canada residing within a circular area of 40 miles in diameter, the centre of which must either be the place of publication or some point not more than 20 miles distant therefrom according to the choice of the publishers. Such papers may also be delivered free to subscribers at the office at which they have been posted, except in cities where the letter carrier system is established. In the latter case ordinary transient newspaper rates are charged.
It will therefore be seen that the weekly press has some privileges? At the request of the weekly newspaper publishers we have given them a substantial reduction. If the hon. gentleman compares the Canadian postal rates with those of Europe or America he will And that we lead these countries in the cheapness of rates. I believe that soon I will be able to grant
the weekly press what its representatives asked for when they met me recently; that Is to say, the weeklies can be sent to a post office on the border and thence distributed in the mails in the United States without paying any additional postage, thus the rate instead of being four cents a pound will be something like two cents a pound or only one cent more than is now paid by the daily press. The question is now engaging the attention of the post office departments at Washington and Ottawa and I expect to be able to make an early announcement with regard to it.
If the minister had appointed a board of censors for papers coming into this country would he not have reached the same end without putting the Canadian press to all this expense and trouble ?

We give respectable American papers the remailing privilege by which they can be mailed to a Canadian post office and thence sent broadcast through the Canadian mails. The undesirable periodicals do not come within our classification. As to the appointment of a board of censors, the burden of the office of Postmaster General is already very great without undertaking the censorship of thousands and thousands of American periodicals. Such American periodicals as Colliers, McClures, and others have applied for and obtained the remailing privilege and are practically obtained by Canadian subscribers at the old rate they paid before the regulations were amended last year.
Do the American agricultural papers come under that privilege ?

As to that, I have been deluged with letters asking to admit a Philadelphia paper which is called, I think the ' Farm.' We have established our rule for second-class matter, and papers coming within that class are described as follows in our postal guide :
Any Canadian newspaper or periodical which, claims to be entitled to a statutory privilege must conform to the following statutory conditions namely:
(aj It must be known as a newspaper or periodical in the generally reoeived sense of the word and consist wholly or in great part of political or other news, or of articles relating thereto, or to other current topics, and be published regularly at intervals of not more than one month.
(b)	The full title, place and date of publication, and the distinguishing number of the issue must he printed on the top of the first and every subsequent page, and also on any paper, print, lithograph or engraving purporting to be a supplement to it, and sent with it.
(c)	It must be addressed to a bona fide subscriber or known newsdealer in Canada.
(d)	It must be delivered into the post office under such regulations as the Postmaster

General may from time to time make for the purpose.
In order to illustrate how some very enterprising American publishing firms are acting, let me point out that as I have just stated, I have been deluged, of late, with letters purporting to be from subscribers to a paper published in Philadelphia, called the ' Farm.'

I would mention the case of the ' Breeders' Gazette,' of Chicago, which is valued very highly by the farmers and agriculturists of Canada. It is a paper that is thought a great deal of by the farmers.

If that paper comes within the definition which I just read to the House, it will certainly receive the privilege granted to the other periodicals. However, this ' Farm,' of Philadelphia, is offered to Canadian subscribers at the rate of 85 cents for five years, published weekly. It almost comes within the definition I have just read. True it is a newspaper, it has a title, it is recognized as a newspaper in the United States, it consists wholly or in great part of articles relating to agriculture or other current topics ; it has a few political opinions, but about three-quarters of the paper is used for advertising purposes. We are told :	Oh, the Post Office Department
is refusing the ' Farm ' the privilege of the mails. It is not a farmers' advocate at all ; it has a few articles bearing on agriculture or agricultural topics, but the balance of the paper, the enormous weight of the paper, is made up of advertisements, of American firms, American pills, American patent medicines. Papers of that quality, under these circumstances, cannot come within the definition which is to be found in our postal guide. Every sensible member of the House will understand why we must resist in some degree the invasion of our Canadian territory by bogus newspapers.
My hon. friend wishes to know how our mails are handled on our railway systems. I regret that he did not give me notice of this question this morning, so that I could speak more definitely and precisely on this technical question; when my estimates come up I will be able to give my hon. friend figures, and, I think, gratify his curiosity. The subsidy which we pay to the various railway systems for the carriage of our mails is based on the mileage. In the United States it is based partly on the poundage, the weight of the mails, and partly on the space which the mail occupies in the postal cars. There is the radical difference between the American and the Canadian railway mail service. It is admitted by experts that the Canadian system is far superior. so much so that I may later furnish to my hon. friend a report which was prepared for the Postmaster General of the United States not long ago, showing the enormous amount of money paid to the railways of the Mr. LEMIEUX.
United States which was admittedly wasted money. I am assured by my expert officials who are quite an authority on this question, that before long the United States will adopt our system of subsidies based on the mileage. I may say that our great trunk systems, the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Grand Trunk Railway and to some extent the Canadian Northern, are complaining that they are not sufficiently paid. On two or three different occasions, independent commissions, composed of experts, were appointed to readjust the payment of the subsidies, and I wish to inform the hon. gentleman that only a few days ago, at the urgent request of my late lamented friend, Mr. Drinkwater, of the Canadian Pacific Railway, Mr. Wainwright, of the Grand Trunk, and the representatives of the Canadian Northern, I signed an order in council asking for the appointment of a commission of experts in order to readjust the payment of the subsidies to our Canadian system. I do not know if that commission will report in favour of an increased subsidy or a reduced one, but it is the custom every fifteen or twenty years, to readjust the subsidy for our railway mail service. It will be admitted that distances in our country are very great and settlement is sparse, mails have increased, and conditions may call for a readjustment.
My hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) also referred to the 1-cent drop letter system. I have stated on different occasions that this question is under consideration. If I may speak personally, I may say that my sympathies are in favour of the 1-cent drop letter. It may be said at once that I am doing something for the cities to which the rural parts of the country are also entitled. There is some truth in that apparently, but when you come to sift the question to the very bottom and see the enormous amount of money which the Post Office Department is losing every day in all the large cities by the establishment and operation of the messenger services, it is quite easy for the postal authorities to realize on the other hand that if we did establish that 1-cent rate for the drop letter in cities and towns, we would at once cause a large increase in our revenue which would enable the department to give to the rural section of the community greater frequency of service than it now has, and more post offices. I may say to my hon. friend, and I state it before the House and the country, that my policy as Postmaster General is to bear in mind my position as trustee on behalf of the people of Canada for the very buoyant revenue of the Post Office Department. I am trustee for that surplus, just as I am a trustee for the moneys of the public which come into the Post Office Savings Department, and it is my duty to be more careful of that money than I am supposed to be of my own money. Therefore, I

must not waste that money. But with our boyant revenue; I feel that I am in a position to give the country an expansion of the service; where we have a weekly or a bi-weekly service, I think I am quite justified in giving a tri-weekly or a daily service. I believe that I should give the public in the thickly peopled portions of the country the service to which they are entitled. I am giving according to circumstances, a daily service, or a semi-daily service. As regards post offices, a few years ago the general policy of the department was to establish at a distance of five or six miles. I have reduced that distance so that, when an application is made to the department, whether made from this side of the House or from the other side, when circumstances justify it, new post offices are granted at a distance of two miles. I intend to continue that policy, and I hope that in doing so, I shall receive the support of the House.
My hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) mentioned the fact that the department had thought it advisable last year to purchase a mail tender for the transatlantic mails. I do not care to eulogize myself, but I may be allowed to say that, if in anything I am entitled to praise by the maritime and commercial interests of the country, it is because I have authorized the purchase of a new steamer for our mail service at Ri-mouski and Sydney. Those who travel to Europe, and as good Canadians and good patriots return to Canada via the St. Lawrence route, have been simply shamed by the mail service as it existed at Rimouski. The first thing sighted by the newcomers or passengers returning to this country was something like a tug coming out to meet the steamer, with hardly any accommodation for passengers, with no' place for the mails; and sometimes this tug could not come to meet the steamer on time and so mails were missed, passengers were incommoded and the reputation of Canada suffered. The first delegation to meet me after I. was appointed Postmaster General was a delegation of the Board of Trade and shipping federation asking me to establish a mail service at Rimouski that would be a credit to the country. I said that I had just been sworn in and did not understand the conditions of the case, but that I would call at Rimouski and see what could be done. I went to Rimouski, and, Mr. Speaker, if you were to return there to-day, you would see what creditable changes have taken place. First, I asked the Public Works Department to give us a wharf worthy of the name, to give us electric light and to give us sheds for the passenger and freight -there were no sheds before. Also, you will gee there to-day, one of the finest steamers in the government fleet, the 1 Lady Evelyn.' That steamer was purchased not by myself-I am not an expert on steamers or on what pertains to steamers ; but, last year, after asking a vote from parliament
for that specific object, and having received it without opposition from either side of the House, I sent to England one of the most trusted officers of the Post Office Department, Mr. Laschinger, the assistant deputy minister. Mr. Laschinger is not an expert either, but he is a very safe and trusted employee. Under my instructions, he went straight to the Canadian High Commissioner, Lord Strathcona, by whom he was referred to the British admiralty, and, under the guidance of the Admiralty officers, lie bought the ' Lady Evelyn,' paying $60,000 or thereabouts. As to the value of the steamer, I can say to my hon. friend that not once, not twice, but ten times or more, I have been told by members of the Shipping Federation of Montreal that I could sell the ' Lady Evelyn ' at about one-third more than it cost the department to obtain her. My hon. friend is misinformed when he says that this boat has missed the mails. On the contrary, the ' Lady Evelyn ' was performing-under another name, I must say-in England, the same service that she is performing at Rimouski, except that the distance she covered on her route in England was longer. She has a fine deck for the mails and splendid accommodation for passengers. I was much pleased last year at the first trip of the ' Lady Evelyn,' when she met the ' Empress of Britain ' at Rimouski. The first man that I sighted on the deck of the ' Empress of Britain ' was the Principal of McGill, who usually goes to England once a year. He said : ' At last you have done away with our national shame, the ' Rhoda,' and I am proud today to come into Canadian waters and find decent accommodation for passengers.' The hon. member for East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) says that the ' Lady Evelyn ' has a crew of from 20 to 25 men. Yes ; the vessel is manned and equipped as an ocean mail tender for Canada ought to be. I keep the men the whole year round, for the service is intended not only for Rimouski but also for Sydney. Could I find and equip a suitable crew for every trip? The vessel may be at Sydney now, but in a few weeks she will be back at Rimouski. Am I to change the crew at every trip ? Could I hope in such a way to secure a well-trained, suitably-dressed crew of men, doing their duty faithfully at very reasonable cost ? I heard some derisive ' Hear, hear,' from my hon. friend from East Sim-coe (Mr. Bennett). Does he suspect that there is something nasty about the ' Lady Evelyn ?' I would like the hon. gentleman to look over the blue-book, to move for any returns or reports he pleases ; I invite him to come with me and pay a visit to the ' Lady Evelyn.' I have been in New York and Liverpool, and I can tell the hon. gentleman that he will see, not merely the best mail tender in Canada, but the best on this continent.
May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) a question? Could he give us the yearly cost ot' this tender ? The boat she replaced cost only $4,000 a year.

Yes, we had a contract with the Captain of the ' Rhoda,' a contract for five years at $4,000 a year! What does that represent as interest ? It represents the interest at G per cent on about $70,000. Now, this boat cost about $60,000. This represents an Interest charge of about $3,600 a year. So, we have saved money on that account. Besides it is right that this mail tender should be the property of the Post Office Department, so that she may be under our orders. And my hon. friend may rest assured that, as regards this steamer, there will be no scandal. The officers of the department here in Ottawa are looking carefully into the accounts for every purchase made in connection with the vessel. My hon. friend may rest assured that they will make it a point to see that the ship is well manned, well equipped and well run-and without scandal.
I was merely asking for information. I wished to learn, if I could, what was the yearly expenditure of this boat.

I think that, the other day, there was a question on the Order Paper on that very subject. In reply to that question, I gave the figures for last year. I have forgotten those figures at present. The expenditure for the present year is just beginning. But if later on when the estimates come up my hon. friend will put the same question, he will have the figures, and he will learn that the amount spent on that steamer is very moderate. Now the hon. gentleman says :	Why is it that the
' Lady Evelyn ' arrived last year in the month of May and was put on the route only late in August ? The answer is very easy. The wharf at Rimouski is a very long- one, yet I regret to say that there was not at the extremity of the wharf a sufficient depth of water for that steamer. We had to do some dredging in the clian-lie] and as soon as the dredging was completed the boat was put on the route. Now the hon. gentleman says : ' I am told that during the time this steamer was performing her usual service the minister used her for himself and his friends.' My hon. friend is misinformed. I may, however, make a confession. I used the steamer twice. First, when the Prime Minister arrived from Europe. I was asked by the members of the press, and by several of my colleagues in the House, members on this side and I think there were two or three on the other side-to meet the Prime Minister near Berthier in the county of Bellechasse. The run lasted three or four hours, and the dinner offered to the Mr. LEMIEUX.
party was at the expense of the Postmaster General. So there was not much expense, the steamer had to be under steam in any case, because she was expected to be called to Rimouski at any day. On one other occasion I used the steamer with the deputy Postmaster General, Mr. Coulter, and my secretary, because I was anxious to establish a winter mail service between the island of Anticosti and the mainland. We left on a Monday afternoon, and on Wednesday morning we were back at Rimouski wharf. But this was an official visit made in the interest of the department and of the service ; and when the minister uses the steamer on occasions like this, I do not think the hon. gentleman should begrudge him the honour of travelling on the ' Lady Evelyn.'
I do not suppose my hon. friend meant to impute to me any thing unworthy in that regard.
Now about free rural mail delivery, I do not know that I should be called upon this evening to speak at length on this question. I would prefer to speak on it later on when the estimates are taken up. However, as the hon. gentleman has spoken on this question during my absence, he is entitled to a statement from me. On one or two different occasions I think he has spoken on this subject during this session. I read the speech delivered by the hon. gentleman in the debate on the address. His plea on that occasion was, in my opinion, a plea in favour of the United States. I sincerely hope that before long when the country is well settled, when immigrants are not prevented from coming to this country-we will have, as the United States have to-day, the luxury of free rural mail delivery. I agree with the hon. gentleman that the United States today are probably acting wisely in establishing free rural mail delivery. But how have they been able to obtain that luxury ff not by their accumulated wealth, by their large population, and by the large revenue yielded by the post office service ? Mr. Speaker, I think the question can be solved in a very few minutes. I need not go to Washington, as my hon. friend says he did. True, my officials went to Washington, but they did not go for the only purpose of obtaining from the United States officials the statement that the system was a success. They went there to investigate. Their minds were unbiased on the subject, they did not come back with the same report as the hon. gentleman. The hon. gentleman went to Washington for the purpose of convincing himself that it was a good thing for Canada to have free rural mail delivery. My officials went to Washington with an unbiased mind in order to investigate, and see for themselves if the conditions prevailing in the two countries were sufficiently alike to allow of the same system being established in Canada, and if it could be work-I ed out as well here as across the frontier.

Six*, the population of the United States, in round numbers, is 80,000,000 ; the postal revenue of the United States Is $183,000,000. In Canada we have not yet a population of
7,000,000. Our limited revenue-I say limited advisedly, although we have a fair surplus-our total gross revenue amounts to $9,000,000. Thus the United States have a population fourteen times ours, with a revenue twenty times as great. Can they not therefore afford themselves the luxury of free rural mail delivery ? Sir, it is with such facts in our minds that this question must be faced. Besides, we have about the same area as the United States. My hon. friend is advocating free rural mail delivery, which I myself would like to see under certain conditions, which conditions I hope will materialize before long. But will my hon. friend say this evening before the province of Ontario and the provinces further west, that he is prepared to discriminate in this matter ? Will he say before the representatives of the western provinces, where the distances are long, the area large and the population sparse-will he say :	You shall
not have free rural mail delivery, but we .will give it to Ontario and to Quebec where the country is more thickly settled ? Why, Sir, my hon. friend could not live twenty-four hours in the Post Office Department if he were to propound such a policy as that regarding the west.
What better position will the people be in ? Will we not have scattered districts a hundred years hence, or fifty years hence, just similar to those we have to-day ?

Is my hon. friend serious ? Does he propose to check immigration ? Does he think this country will not become settled ? Will he pretend, having read the history of Canada, that a hundred years ago the country was as thickly settled as it is to-day ? Is it not a fact that a hundred years ago in the province of Ontario not far from this city of Ottawa, there were no inhabitants ? Ottawa Itself, though now thickly settled, was but a solitude seventy or eighty years ago. My hon. friend surely does not expect that the aggressive provinces of the west will remain unsettled. On the contrary, I think they are God's heritage, and it is predicted that before long the balance of power will pass from the east to the west. Then my hon. friend will, if he lives in that golden age, realize ,that the west was entitled to the same treatment as the east.
Would the minister give me some reason why the thickly settled portions of eastern Canada should not be taken into consideration, and the thickly settled portions of the west as well ?

Because a farmer from Scandinavia or Germany happens to settle near Edmonton, or near that ambitious city of Strathcona, should he receive more consideration from the Post Office Department than the brave settler who goes upon the distant prairie and settles boldly alone ? I say that the same treatment must be given to the isolated farmer as to the farmer residing near the city or town.
Why is it, when advantages are given to the cities, that the rural districts are not taken into consideration at the present moment.

No intelligent resident of, say Buckingham, would claim that he is entitled, as regards letter carrier service, to the same service as a resident of Ottawa gets. The parallel should not be established in that sense, but I say that as regards free rural mail delivery-I am not speaking of city delivery

the same treatment should be given to the sparsely populated section of the country as to the thickly settled section of the country. Mark well, I am speaking of the farming community. My hon friend asks : Why do you not imitate the United States in this matter ? My hon. friend should not ignore the fact that the system of free rural mail delivery existed before the United States adopted it. The United States adopted free rural mail delivery, when? When they had 6,000,000 people? Not at all. They did not adopt rural free mail delivery with 15,000,000, nor with 20,000,000 nor with 60,000,000 people. They never dreamed of it in those days; not even when the population reached 70,000,000, but the United States started free rural mail delivery when the population reached the high watermark of 80,000,000 and when their revenue had increased from a few million dollars to $175,000,000. This system is not an American discovery. My hon. friend should hot lose sight of the fact that free rural mail delivery has existed for years and years in Europe. In Great Britain, for instance, where from Liverpool to London, it is practically one row of houses on both sides of the railway systems. It exists in France and in Belgium. But what is Belgium compared with Saskatchewan, with Manitoba, or even with Prince Edward Island ? We could put three Belgiums, and even more, in one of the smaller provinces of the Dominion. Therefore we must, before thinking of establishing that costly system in Canada, realize that we have an area as vast as that of the United States of America, that on the other hand we have only 7,000,000 of a population as against 85,000,000 in the United States, and that we have only a gross postal revenue of $9,000,000 as against one in the United States of $183,000,000. Further than that we have not the same climatic conditions. That fact must be taken into consideration also.

Whilst in the United States, generally speaking, they have a fair climate all the year round and good roads, we must admit that in certain sections of the country, during even the month of April and during several months of the year, our roads are practically impassable. All these facts must be taken into consideration before advocating the establishment of such a luxury. Let me draw a parallel. Here is an individual with a revenue of $50,000 a year ; my hon. friend from Montreal, St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), for instance, whom I see in his seat, has, I presume, at least a revenue of $50,000 a year. My hon. friend from East Lambton (Mr. Armstrong), less fortunate, has only a revenue of $5,000 a year. Both are well off according to their relative condition of life. Surely my hon. friend from St. Antoine could buy an automobile and every morning he could be conveyed from his private house or country residence to his office, whilst the hon. member from Lambton would be satisfied to take, as I do myself, the tramway, or his bicycle or the ordinary train. He would see my hon. friend from St. Antoine passing in his automobile, whirling about in the streets of Montreal or suburbs, thus attracting his attention. Suppose the hon. member for St. Antoine would remonstrate with him and say: Why do you not get an automobile? You will get a drive through the fresh air ; your health will be better and besides it lends more dignity and charm to life to drive in an automobile? Would not my hon. friend from Lambton at once answer :	' It is a question of
revenue ; you have $50,000, you reside in the country, so do I, but I have only $5,000, I have a large family and I must be satisfied with the tramway.' So it is with free rural mail delivery. We have the United States on one side, same area as Canada, but with a revenue of $182,000,000. Here is Canada on the other, same area as the United States, but with only a postal revenue of $9,000,000 a year. Can we indulge a drive in the automobile of free rural mail delivery ? Evidently not, Mr. Speaker, we must be satisfied to live within our means. We must be as wise, as prudent as my hon. friend from Lambton would be if his revenue were what I have just mentioned as a comparison. Now, the United States are spending an enormous amount on this free rural mail delivery system. Last year, according to the figures which we have in the department, the postal authorities spent $26,000,000; that is to say, one-seventh of their income. But this is, Mr. Speaker, and my hon. friend should realize it, three times the total gross revenue of the Canadian Post Office Department. If Canada ceased to spend one red cent on its railway mail service, ceased to pay the postmasters-and what a noise there would be in the country if we did-if we ceased to pay for the conveyance of the mails and Mr. LEMIEUX.
if we used the total gross revenue of the Post Office Department for three years it would barely pay what the United States spent last year on free rural mail delivery. My hon. friend says that it is a revenue producer. Most of the revenue in the Post Office Department is derived from the sale of stamps for letters. Newspapers are carried at a loss by the department. We do it to accommodate the public, but they are carried at a loss. If I had more time I would give figures to the House. We get our revenue from the sale of the little postage stamp, but in order to have buoyancy we must have large centres of population as they have in the United States, large cities-Chicago. New York, Philadelphia and San Francisco-where millions of people are living and then we shall get revenue. We get a limited revenue. Therefore, we can spend only a limited amount of money. Now, does this free rural mail delivery increase the revenue? Has it increased the revenue of the United States Post Office Department? We made an investigation. I do not know if my hon. friend challenges the investigation made by the officers of the Canadian Post Office Department.
I certainly do.

We sent to Washington trusted officials of the department, men like Mr. Ross, of Toronto, nearly 35 years in the service, taking more interest in his public duties than he would take in his own private business, being at present broken in health, because he has travellled during 35 years from one end of the country to the other to see that the Post Office Department was run economically and at the same time in the interest of the public. He went to Washington with Mr. Smith, and not relying alone on what they might hear from politicians who benefited politically by the system, - they remained in Washington for several weeks and made a thorough investigation and report. They reported that on 81 routes selected by the United States postal authorities for their examination, the revenue has increased during the six months by $50 ; on 51 other routes there had been no increase in revenue, and on 132 routes there had been a diminution of $225. This is not a flight of the imagination, these are cold facts, and before telling the good people of Ontario that there should be rural free delivery it is well that the facts should be presented. Now, the people of Quebec would be quite willing to have rural free delivery too. Even on the distant shores of Gaspd where they have received so many good things from the government since 1890. the hardy fishermen there would be quite willing to have free rural mail delivery. What my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) claims for Ontario I would be disposed to claim for Quebec, but to be fair and just to the other provinces of the Dominion I would

think that British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, are just as much entitled to that luxury as the two large provinces.
And the Yukon.

Well, if we had gathered from the Yukon the crop of gold which the member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) said were there when he combated that famous railway project, we might have been able to stand the expense of free rural mail delivery, but we did not get the gold and so we must be satisfied with our gross postal revenue of $9,000,000 a year. There is no evidence that in the United States, free rural mail delivery has materially increased the revenue. According to the report of our officials to which I have referred, during a period of six months in 1903, on 132 routes 3,638,000 pieces were delivered, and in 1904, during the same period, 3,662,899, showing an increase of 2,651 pieces or seven-hundredths of one per cent. And this was on 132 routes which were pointed out by the United States postal authorities as being the best routes in the whole Union. My hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) should know that the free rural delivery in the United States which was initiated at an expense of a few thousand dollars, cost the country last year the fabulous sum of $37,000,000. When the hon. gentleman goes before the electors of Lambton with his pleasant smile and condemns this government for refusing them that luxury of rural free delivery which the people across the border enjoy ; when he tells them that the Canadian Post Office Department has no care for the welfare of the farmers of Lambton, I wish he would also tell them that the rural free delivery in the United States cost last year $37,000,000. If the hon. gentleman would invite me to his county I would like to discuss that matter with his friends, and I am sure they would give me a cordial reception when I disclosed to them these cold facts.
Until 1904, the United States published figures as to the cost of the routes and the amount of revenue derived therefrom. Since that date no official figures have been published. In 1904, the result of rural free delivery for the whole of the United States, setting forth the total number of letters, post cards, papers, circulars, packages, collected from all the routes and the total amount of stamps cancelled on all the routes and the revenue collected from rural free delivery, shows, there was collected one hundred and thirty-three odd million pieces at a cost of $12,681,876, and yielding a revenue of $2,601,815, thus giving a deficit, so far as rural free delivery is concerned, in that year of $10,080,061. The United States since that date have published no statistics until the present year when they have published a statement in their annual report of 2.31
the results, not of the whole service but of twenty-seven of the best and most favourable routes in the United States. But the report states that the" statement is for the purpose of giving some indication (mark you) of the possibilities of rural free delivery in tlie more densely populated localities served, both suburban and rural. The hon. gentleman complained in the debate on the address that I had stated the United States deficit on this service to be about $20,000,000. I do not remember having made that statement, but I may point out to the hon. gentleman that at a recent congress of the postmasters of the United States, attended by 1,500 postmasters, matters concerning the postal service in the United States were discussed and amongst others the possibility of developing the rural free delivery system by extending parcel post delivery on the routes, and the statement was then made and it has not been contradicted so far as I know, that the rural free delivery service cost $35,000,000 a year and only yielded a revenue of $5,000,000, thus leaving an annual deficit of $30,000,000, which is $10,000,000 more than the amount I am alleged to have stated. The hour is late and I shall conclude by thanking my hon. friend (Mr. Armstrong) for his courteous treatment of the department. We may differ, but I must admit that when he discussed questions in connection with the Post Office Department he is always very fair indeed. I am glad he has brought these several matters to my notice this evening and when the estimates are being considered we may discuss the question again. I am sincere in telling my hon. friend that I am as anxious as he can be to give the people of Canada an improved postal service, although I must say that we have on the whole a most creditable system in the urban and suburban districts. Above all, we must not exceed our revenue.
