I am as anxious as he is to give the farmers of Canada a free rural mail delivery, but my hon. friend will never convince a farmer of the west that he should pay for a luxury'to be given only to the farmers of the east. He will never convince a man with a head on his shoulders and with common sense in the head that we are in a position to spend as much money with our limited revenue and our small population as the United States with their enormous revenue and their large population.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a word in reply.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has no right to reply. The only motion before the House is to go into Supply.
I am sorry I have not the opportunity of making just a few remarks.

I wish to ask the Minister of Finance a question. I shall



first read the following resolution which was sent to me to-day:
The Women's Christian Temperance Union of Brampton passed the following resolution:
Whereas we understand that a Bill is being nrepared for the House of Commons of the Dominion of Canada to prohibit the manufacture and sale of cigarettes;
Resolved, that, for the sake of the youth of our country, we sincerely hope and pray that such a measure may receive the most hearty support both of the Commons and of the Senate of Canada, and soon become law in our Dominion.
I would ask the Finance Minister if a Bill is being prepared by the government to be introduced during this session respecting cigarettes?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I must admit that I am unable to give my bon. friend any definite information. The whole question has been engaging the attention of the ministers as well as of other hon. members of the House, and it may be that before the close of the session some legislation, perhaps not altogether as broad as my hon. friend suggests, but approaching the same lines, will be introduced. I am not in a position to make a more definite statement at present.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Chicoutimi post office, $7,500.

speakeroldname: Hon. WM. PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works).
speechtext:
This is a revote to make provision for the completion of a public building now under erection at Chicoutimi.
Mr. FOWLER, How much has been spent?
Up to November 15, $28,728.
What is the contract price?
$22,472, not including electric wiring, heating, interior fittings or clock.
How about the duty on that clock?

I have no information as to that. In the case of the clock of which we spoke the other day, I find there were several tenders for the clock and the tenderer to whom the tender was awarded tendered for a certain amount, duty not included. Therefore, of course, the duty had to be added to his contract price.
And that was expressly stated in the tender?

Yes. I feel that I should inform the committee that my deputy was mistaken in regard to the security for the Halifax custom house. He told me that the security was still held by the de- I Mr. BLAIN. '
partment, but on inquiry he finds that he was mistaken in regard to that. The security was paid over before I became minister and also before he became acting deputy minister. We have held back some $3,000 or $4,000 of the main bill.

By whose authority was
the security paid over?

The certificate the department had at that time was that the building was substantially completed, and it was felt that it was not necessary to retain the security longer. It was paid over in the early part of 1907.
Referring to the confidential report of Mr. Dodwell on the Halifax building and the subsequent report of Mr. Wright, to what extent do they agree?
In a general way the report of Mr. Wright does not go to the same extent as the report of Mr. Dodwell.
Under the circumstances do you not think the reports should be produced ?
1 could not produce a confidential report without the consent of the writer.
Was it expressely understood between you and Mr. Dodwell that the report should be confidential.
Mr. Dodwell desired that it should be confidential.
Had the minister not a right to direct the making of that report? Mr. Dodwell is an officer of the department.

I thought he would write more freely if the report was confidential. He has general supervision over all matters in that section of the country, but he was not in direct charge of this building and, therefore, the report was made confidential.

He has general supervision over all matters in that section of the country, and I cannot see why Mr. Bush did not report to him and why Dodwell found it necessary to have verbal communication with the minister. I do not understand the supervision exercised by Mr. Dodwell. The minister had a right to command him to make a report. I cannot say that the minister has acted quite properly with regard to this matter. He does not seem to entertain the right idea with regard to the duties of the-officers of his department.

Was the statement correct that was made the other evening, that the government had paid duty of over $400 on the coat of arms supplied for the Halifax building which should have been paid by the contractor under the contract ?

The statement made has been verified with regard to the duty upon the coat of arms.
Cookshire public building, $5,000.
The minister promised to bring some information with regard to the granolithic sidewalk before the Antigon-ish building.

I have the information. The sidewalk cost 26 cents per square foot, which included the levelling. Mr. Ewart, the chief architect, says that that was the cheapest price at which he could get it done In that locality.

Let us have the dimensions. For, I must say, 1 have not the confidence in the chief architect's figures I would like to have. If the lot was of the dimensions stated by the minister and the sidewalk was of reasonable width, it would be impossible to make up the amount of money paid in this case.
A portion of the sidewalk was 21 feet. The architect says that the price of granolithic pavement in Ottawa is 18 cents. In some places it is more, in some less.
Not long ago in our section of country this kind of work was done at 9 cents in one case and at 11 cents in another.
The chief architect says that he has had this work done at as low as 11 cents, but 26 cents was the lowest price he could get in Antigonish.
But I would like the dimensions.
The chief architect brought the plan over before, but he has not it with him this evening. He will bring it.
Well, with the plan before us, we can discuss the matter.
This vote of $5,000 is for a public building in Cookshire. The site has been given free at the cost of the municipal council.
What did the site at Chicoutimi cost ?
At whose suggestion was this vote for the Cookshire building put in the estimates ?
The people of Cookshire asked for the building and the municipal council passed a resolution to furnish the site free to the Crown.
Has tne building been commenced ?
No.
What is it to cost ?
It is expected to cost in the neighbourhood of $19,000 or $20,000.
What is the size of Cookshire ?
About 2,000 population, I am informed. It is a growing town, I believe-a nice town.

The minister did not answer my question. I asked at whose request this item of $5,000 was put in the estimates ? He says that the municipal council gave the site and the people of the town asked for the building. In what way did they ask-by petition ?
A resolution passed by the council was sent to the Minister of Public Works in the ordinary way.

Has the minister a copy ?
Mr. PUGSLEY, I have not it with me.

And as to the town generally ?
Mi'. PUGSLEY. A petition was sent in by the residents and ratepayers of the town, which was transmitted by the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Hunt), on December 6, 1907.
Has the minister a copy of the petition ?
No. It would make a bulky assortment of papers if I should bring the petitions for all these public buildings.
I did not ask for all, but only for one.
But I did not know which one the hon. gentleman would ask for.
The census of 1901 gives Cookshire a population of about 800.
It has grown a good deal since. Then, I understand, this post office will serve a thickly settled community besides that included within the municipal limits of the town.
What is the revenue ?

For the nine months, 1906-7, the revenue was $2,128.44 ; money orders issued $12,902 ; money orders paid, $8,411. Then, to give an idea of the business of the place, the exports were $297,079 in the nine months of the last fiscal period ; imports $65,047. Of course, this building is for a custom house as well.
It is not a sub-port, is it?
It must be, because the customs duties collected at the post office amount to about $2,000.

I am not finding fault with this public building for Cookshire, which is a nice, thriving little town. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) has taken it under his paternal wing and given it a post office, and we are wicked enough to suspect that he has an ulterior motive.
You must not impute motives.

I say we ' suspect.' If the people of Cookshire get the advantage of this building, so much the better for them. But I wish to press upon the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) the fact that if he contends that Cookshire is entitled to a post office by reason of its importance, the amount of its revenue and the business done, he has double reason for giving a post office to the town of Hillsborough, in the county of Albert.
I am glad that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fowler) approves of this.
My attitude is merely negative-I do not disapprove.

I would refer to the census of 1901, page 302. I am not objecting to the post office for Cookshire, but I wish to show that the population must have increased rapidly if it has 2,000 now. According to the census of 1902 there were 322 English, 80 Irish, 49 Scotch, 1 of other nationality, 338 French-total population 801.
That is within the municipal limit. But I am told that there is an important community besides to be served.
How far does the minister go in order to find his population of 2,000 ?
I do not understand whether the hon. gentleman (Mr. Armstrong) is opposed to this or in favour of it.

I am not speaking to oppose this vote. I am only saying that if the minister proposes to give a twenty thousand dollar post office to every town of 801 population, we would like to know it, that is all.
My opinion is that a good deal depends on the importance of the place and on the business.
Will the minister tell us what the present post office costs the country for rent and light, and If there is any other government building there ?

I am not sure whether there is an inland revenue office there, but there is a custom house. This building will be also used for customs. The rent paid last year was $190 for the post office and customs office.

We proposed to put up a building costing $19,000, that will cost Mr. PUGSLEY.
us about $1,100 a year, I presume, after it is built.
The intention of the town council is to rent a portion of the building for a registry office; that will give a little income.

I do not think that is a proper thing to do. It seems to me it is a great mistake for this government, to put up a building for federal purposes and rent a portion of it to a municipality. Let the municipality build its own registry office.

It is not considered undesirable for municipalities to rent portions of public buildings which are not required for municipal offices. That was a proposition which the municipal council made, and rent might be got from that. I do not see any objection to it at the present time.
Could the minister give the date of the resolution of the municipal council ?
It was forwarded on December 6, 1907.
When was this $5,000 first placed in the estimates?
Last year.
This is a full customs port. Mr. Ross is collector there.
The amount received from customs was $3,186.
Is it the policy of the department to appropriate public money for the construction of registry offices for municipalities ? Surely that is a new departure on the part of the government.

I thought I made myself clear that it had not yet been decided whether to rent a portion of the building as a registry office. But the town council urged that, as it was a very convenient site for that purpose, when the building was erected there might be made in it a room which could be used for the registry office, and for which of course, the council would pay rent.
Have you got the request there ? I would like to see it.
The town council has nothing to do with the registry office, it is the county council.

The Information I have is that the resolution was passed by the municipal council of the town of Cookshire. They made a gift of the site, and they have also urged that in the erection of the building, as this is a very convenient site and in a public park, it would be desirable that provision should be made for a

registry office, for which they would pay rental.	[DOT]

The minister has gone further than that, he has intimated that in his opinion that is all right. The minister might just as well provide at the expense of the federal government, a court house and jail as to provide a registry office. I venture to say there is not another instance like it in Canada. I protest strongly against any such departure from the rule. Does the Minister of Agriculture, for instance, think that is a proper thing ?
All we are asking for now, is a vote for the building ; the question of the registry office is one that we will have to consider.
Who will consider it ?
The minister.
The minister has already decided.

No, I said where a town council is willing to give a convenient site in a square, as apparently this is, and if they request that in erecting the building there should be one room made suitable for a registry office for which they are willing to pay an adequate rent, there may be cases that would be entirely justifiable. Whether it will be done in this instance, I am not prepared to say.

Was that the condition on which the site was granted ?
the municipal council and the petition by the residents of the town.

We are embarking on a new principle, a principle that, I think, will be admitted by most people, is a bad one. If a place does not require as large a building it is an easy matter to reduce the amount that is proposed to be voted for that purpose. But, when we have supplied a place with a custom house, an inland revenue office and a post office, I think we have gone as far as we can reasonably expect to go.
Will the minister supply, at a future date, the petition and resolution passed by the municipal council?
I will be very glad to do so.
And would the minister say wnether any part of the building will be constructed for a registry office?
I will look at the resolution and I have no objection at all to stating my views later on.
Then we will have an opportunity of discussing this item again?
Not this item, but you can discuss the principle on some other item.
When will that building be commenced?
We hope just as soon as the plans and specifications can be prepared and tenders called for.
There was no condition.
I think the minister ought to bring down that resolution of the town council to which he pays so much attention.

I think we should have that resolution. The minister has pointed out that this building was put up at the request of the municipal council, and by a petition of the residents. He says he sees no objection to using a portion of this building for a registry office.
ilr. PUGSLEY. Provided they pay for it.

Provided they pay for it. In other parts of Canada, particularly in Ontario, no such thing -would be tolerated for a moment. Every county council must provide a suitable registry office for the requirements of the country. It would not be suggested for a moment that the government should provide such a building; in fact, a building of this kind would be of no value unless the building were constructed especially for that purpose. It is rather unfair for the minister to come down and ask for an appropriation without having under his hand the request that was made by
Dominion public buildings-renewals, improvements, repairs, &c., $20,000.

This vote of $20,000 is to be applied in carrying out renewals, repairs and work of that kind generally to public buildings in Quebec for which special appropriations have not been made. This is the ordinary maintenance vote which is passed every year.
Mi-. FOWLER. At what places is it expected to do this work?

At some twenty or thirty different places and the repairs range from $4 up to $2,000.
Dundee custom house-renewals and repairs, $1,800.
When was that building erected?
It was built 58 years ago, and these repairs are absolutely necessary.
What repairs are being made?
There is to be a new stone foundation, the building is to be raised three and a half feet, there will be 175 running feet of concrete and some excavating.
Does the minister know that this is a very old house that this $1,800 is being spent on, and that he could erect a new building for that sum of money?

I know it is an old
house, but with these repairs it may last some time yet.
But with the $1,800 which is being spent upon it now you can put up a new building.
I would not like to try to put up a new building with $1,800.
You could add a little to it and make a good building.
I see this is a revote. Mr. PUGSLEY. It is a revote.
If the money was voted last year and not spent there is no very great need for it.
The contract has now been let.

Who has the contract?
-Air. PUGSLEY. Mr. J. Fraser.
Air. BERGERON AVere tenders called for?
It is going to cost altogether $3,300.
How many tenders were there?
I think Mr. Fraser was asked to tender; there was no public call by advertisement for tenders.
Do I understand the minister to say that it is going to cost $3,30 j?
Yes.
Why are you asking for only $1,S00?

We are asking simply for $1,S00 because there was $1,800 granted last year. The repairs have not been started. This is a revote, but it is not unlikely that I may ask for $1,500 more in the supply estimates so as to get sufficient to do the work this year.
Farnkam post office-alterations, including rearrangement of fittings, $5,500.
This is a revote to make provision for alterations, including a rearrangement of the interior fittings. This has been requested by the Post Office Department.
When was the Farn-ham office built?
What are the alterations? Air. PUGSLEY.
It is proposed to make a larger lobby for the accommodation of the public and to change the interior fittings.	-

The usual way is for the minister to state how much is to be expended on each item of the repairs, what is to be done with the money, so much for this alteration and so much for that. The minister is not following the usual custom of the Department of Public Works.
This memorandum has been prepared by the same gentleman who has for twenty or thirty years been preparing these statements.
I have been here for twenty years and I have always heard the minister get up and read off in detail an estimate of all the different items, it is placed on ' Hansard ' and we can read it.
That is done in some cases where it is asked for.
It is always done. When we ask what he is going to do with this money he tells us in detail. This explanation which consists in stating that a room is to be enlarged is no explanation at all.
AYhat will be the whole amount of expenditure?
And it is a revote?
Yes.
Will these repairs be made by contract?
They will probably be made by contract.
Are they all interior repairs?

What kind of repairs are they?
Air. PUGSLEA'. There has been some question as to what should be the extent of the repairs and the details have not yet been determined on by the chief architect.
Then the estimate appears to be submitted to parliament on guess work, and it is not a businesslike thing to do.

Alore extensive repairs have been urged than are contemplated by the chief architect, and if we make very extensive repairs it would raise a question whether it would not be better to erect a new building.

What did the building cost in the first place?
Air. PUGSLEY'. It has cost altogether for construction and repairs $11,400.
What is the revenue?

Postal revenue (nine months), $2,867 ; money orders issued, $20,000 ; money orders paid, $17,000 ; population, 3,114.
Grosse Isle quarantine station-improvement and repairs to building, $12,500.
These repairs and improvements have been requested by the medical attendant at the station.
Who is responsible for the carrying out of these works?
We have an agent there, Mr. Beiand.
Any relation of the member?
I am told not.

Have you an inspector of works?
Mr. 'PUGSLEY. Mr. Beiand. .

Every year since I have been in this House we have been expending money on this quarantine station.
I have been on the island and everything appears to be in good order and repair, but still we have to spend money every year as if we were compelled to whether it was wanted or not.
Last year there was $12,520 expended. What was that for?
It was for lumber, plumbing, paint, cement, hardware, wages, sundries, &c.
Was the cement purchased by public tender?
I cannot say now, but the quantity purchased was very small.
What is the policy of the department?
The policy is to call for tenders for cement and we are frequently doing so.
I see six rugs were purchased from T. Beiand & Co., at over $20 each. What were they for?
I presume they were for the house of the resident physician.
Was the cement bought by public tender?

This was before my advent to the department and I cannot say just now, but the policy of the department will be to purchase as far as possible all the articles that are required for public buildings by tender. Occasionally there may be small quantities which it would not be convenient to purchase in that way, but as a rule competitive prices will be obtained.
Will this money be expended by contract or by day's work?
While some of it may be done by contract It is probable that the bulk of it would be more economically and perhaps better done by day's work.
Who is the foreman?
Mr. Beiand, the representative of the Public Works Department at Quebec, is supposed to do that.
He lives at Quebec?
When repairs are being made to any extent I understand he remains at Grosse Isle.
During the whole progress of the work?
So I understand.
Is that the real fact?
I understand so. He is supposed to be there sufficiently to have an oversight of the work.
Was he there long last year?

I am told he has been twenty years in that employment.
Grosse Isle quarantine station-disinfecting apparatus, including building, $3,500.
Will that complete the work ?

The chief architect says so. There was an expenditure up to November 30 last year of $4,121.
Mr. BENNETT, What is this for ?
Additional sulphur apparatus is needed there.
IHow much is for disinfecting apparatus and how much for the building ?

The building will cost $4,689, and the balance will be used for the other purpose.
Ivnowlton public building, $4,500.
This is a revote of $4,500 to make provision towards the erection of a public building in Knowlton.
What is the population ?
What would be the total cost ?
The contract has not yet been let, but I suppose that including heating and everything it will be somewhere in the vicinity of $15,000, possibly more.

This money was voted last year. If it was very much needed,

you would suppose it would have been commenced. It looks like holding this money out before the community.
There was difficulty in procuring a site. The site owned by the municipal council and their authority for the sale had to be obtained. The site is about 115 feet by 90 feet, and it cost about |350.
Have you agreed to build a registry office ?
No, but there is to be an armoury in conjunction with the post office building.

To what amount will
the minister bind himself as the outside cost of this building ? If you start to erect buildings in every town or village of 800 the country will be bankrupt.
Knowlton is the county town, there is no public building in the county, and gentlemen opposite recommended me strongly last year, to get a building put there for that reason.

When we remember all the noise and trouble that was raised about the La Prairie post office, by the hon. gentlemen, when in opposition, and then have them vote money for a building of this kind, in a place of the size of Knowlton. it is not extraordinary that the public lose confidence in public men.

It is generally conceded that a county town can very fairly lay claim to a public building and such buildings have been erected in most cases. This is the only public building in the county and the post office accommodation is quite inadequate.
The county town is generally not the largest but the'most central town in the county. Is the largest place in Brome only about 800 ?
We do not spread our villages over half creation. The village itself has a population of 800, but the post office will serve a community of at least 2,000.
What is paid for the present office ?
Eighty dollars a year.
What is the revenue ?
The revenue was $1,557, and the rent paid is $00. That is according to the report.
That is for nine months.
How many are employed on the. post office staff at present ?
The post office postmaster himself. But I think he employs two people in the office.
What has the Finance Minister to say about these expenditures ? Does he allows every place that asks for it to have a public building ? If so, it is no wonder that our expenditure is so high .

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not every place. But I am afraid I am responsible for the doctrine the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) has advanced. I think we can justify the construction of a public building-not necessarily an expensive building-in the county town of every county in which there is no other Dominion public building. I ventured to lay that rule down some years ago, and the more I think of it the more reasonable it seems to me. I think the government owes something to the people of the country in the matter of public buildings. Knowlton is a small town, but, if there is no other public building in the county, I think the government does no wrong in putting up a modest public building in this county town. It is a good example, and while it will cost a little, it does not mean that we are to put a public building in every town-for, I take it, there are other communities in Brome that might put forward a claim. But, if you confine it to the county town of a small county, or, in a larger county extends the rule to two or three communities, I think it is a good rule.

I am sorry, in view of the statement we have just heard, that the hon. member for Sunbury & Queens (Mr. \\ ilmot) is not in his place at the moment, for neither Sunbury nor Queens has a Dominion building. In view of the statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) a claim might very properly be put in for a public building for Oromocto in Sunbury county and for Gagetown in Queens. It is a new doctrine to me that the government will build public buildings in the county town of every county that has no other government building.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have not gone so far as to say that these buildings must all be put up at once. I am not familiar with Oromocto, but I know Gagetown and I think that if there is not a public building in that county a fair claim could be made. And, if hon. gentlemen will be patient, no doubt it will be carried out. But all this will not be done in a day.
What procedure should one take in order to get one of these buildings in his constituency ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Patience is a good policy.

I have seven or eight towns of from 1,200 to 1,800 people without a public building of any description. I have not made any particular request for one. But if the government is willing to build

on such easy conditions, I think my constituency would have a claim.
Which town would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Herron) suggest ?
Well, for instance, Mae-leod. The post office there is unfit for a postal service. And it is a very important town.
What is the population ?
The size of one of our villages.
My hon. friend (Mr. Herron) must have patience. It is twenty-six years since I commenced to represent Brome and the county is only now getting its first public building.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman right in saying that there is no public building in Macleod. I have understood that there is a very considerable building there.

The constituency is about
40,000	square miles.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But I am speaking of the principle of making some public expenditure within a county.
The Minister of Public Works has not said that he will bind himself that this building shall not exceed in cost any particular sum.
I think I can say pro bably it will not be more than $20,000.
Was there a petition for this building ?

No, I asked for it. And the hon. member's (Mr. Reid) desk-mate (Mr. Fowler) also asked for it.
Lachute public building, $10,000.
This is a revote.
In what county is Lachute ?
In Argenteuil. The site has been bought and some work has been done. The total expenditure up to November 30, 1907, was $1,645.68.
From whom was the site bought ?
From Mr. H. M. Gall, for $1,200. It has a frontage of 44 feet on Main street.
Has the contract been let?
Yes, to Messrs. Lafleur & Son, of Lachute.
What is the total estimated cost ?
What is the population of Lachute ?

By the census of 1901, it was 2,022.
Lake Megantic public building, $2,000.
This is to make provision for the purchase of a site. The total cost is $4,000.
How large a place is it ?
In 1901, it had a population of 1,883.
That is an awful price for the lot in a town of that size.
It is a very valuable lot with a frontage of 64 feet on Main street, and a depth of 132 feet to a lane. It was considered a most desirable lot and the owners were not anxious to sell.
Why so big a lot ? In Lachute you have a lot of only 44 feet frontage ?

We could not vei'y well have the lot split up, as the owners would not sell in that way. The land was owned by the Presbyterian church, and, of course, they would not want to sell part of the lot.
Levis public building, $10,000.
Is there not already a post office at L6vis ?
This is for a new building. The total probable cost is $49,713.44.
When was it commenced ?
Is it not finished yet?
The architect tells me it is finished and occupied.
Then, what is the money for ?

The total expenditure to 3.1st October last was $35,274.44. Amount due on the contract, $6,262 ; wiring, $750 ; amount due on lock boxes, sidewalk, fencing, &c., $500 ; contingencies, superintendence, $3,163. rl'he first contract was for $22,000. The $49,000 includes many things which are not in the contract.
How does it come to pass that there are $27,000 for extras ?

After the contract was let the site was changed, and that caused a great deal of extra work.
Mr. ,T. D. REID. There was a contract let for a certain sized building. Now it was changed from one site to another. Why did the change of site necessitate so great an additional cost ? if a contract was given for $22,000 and then you turn around

and ask for $37,000 for extras, there must be something wrong. I have no doubt that there is some robbery going on in that case. There is public robbery, I do not hesitate to say it.

X can now give the House .some details of the extra cost. What the chief architect tells me is that after the contract was let it was decided to change the site. Where it was decided to erect the building was upon a place where there was an old wharf. That wharf had all to be cut out and a new foundation built of concrete. There was the extra work of excavating on account of the change of site, which amounted to $552. The concrete work, the brick, and so forth, cost $4,261. Then there was further excavation and concrete, and additional stone, $4,275. Then taking something off the foundation and replacing it, 212 yards, $2,106. There is a little over $11,000. I will give the reason why the site was changed. After the contract was let it became necessary, by reason of the Intercolonial improvements at Levis, to widen the street, and that necessitated putting the post office in a different position by some 50 feet. There was a new station and yard room required. The contract was let in 1905 to Mr. Joseph Couture.
What was the original cost of the site ?
The site was given by the Intercolonial authorities ; the town and railway together owned the land. The government did not pay anything for either the first site or the second site.

The minister said he had to build a post office 50 feet from the first site, but that ought not to change the cost of the site. The government bought some ground there to enlarge the street. I do not see how the minister can claim there was any additional cost for the building.

Suppose the place where the building was to be first erected was solid ground, and suppose that the new site necessitated building part of the foundation where there was an old wharf. That old wharf had to be cut away and a concrete foundation made. Surely that would change the cost.

I do not ask any one to tell me the location of that post office. He says there was a wharf there. I have my doubts whether there ever was a wharf there. I went into that very place sixty years ago and there was no wharf. Afterwards a wharf was built, but outside the place where the post office is now. But where the post office stands there never was a chance to build a wharf because there was no water. At low tide the water Is probably twenty feet from where the post office stands now, and when the tide comes in Mr. J. D. REID.
there is a little water, but not much. There is water at high tide in the month of May. Now will this $2,000 finish that post office?
Mr. rUGSLEY. It will complete it.
Are you sure of that?

One cannot be sure of anything in this world.
Mr. jiORIN. That post office was built on poor ground. There was a post office building bought at St. Thomas, Montmagny, and it went down two years after it was-bought. The government paid $7,794.50 for it. I do not intend to blame the minister for that because he was not in the government at the time. But, when they commenced to erect this building at Levis they built it on a poor foundation, the foundation gave away, another man took the job of fixing it up, it gave way again and they again fixed it up. Now, if you go there and take a sight you see that the first story on the north side of the building caves in about four inches, and the second story leans out about four inches. The building warps and wobbles. The first story leans south and the second leans north. That is why I ask the minister if he knows what it will cost ?

I wish to thank my hon. friend for assisting me in giving information to the committee as to the very great difficulties that have been met with in the construction of this building. What my hon. friend has stated accounts very largely for the large amount of extras which were necessary in the construction of the building. But, every effort, so the chief architect tells me, was made to secure a solid foundation. The building rests upon a concrete foundation that is deemed to be perfect, and there is every reason to believe that the foundation will stand.
Has the minister any personal knowledge of the locality?
Only in a general way.

I do not think the minister is doing himself credit. He knows a great deal about Ldvis. We remember that a few years ago there was a long discussion about a question as to the acquisition of land in Ldvis for the purpose of the Intercolonial Railway. Some parties who owned the land there had met in the department with the statement of an engineer that the land was only worth $1 a foot.
Was that during the construction of the St. Charles branch?
It was while Mr. Blair was minister. Was that the time?
No, prior to that.

Mr. Blair happened to I be the minister at that time and these par-

ties found an adverse report in the department that the land was only worth $1 a foot. By an inspiration they became possessed of the idea that it would be advisable to secure a magic wand to wave over the head of the minister or some other important gentleman, and these parties hied themselves down to the city of St. John and secured the services of one Win. Pugs-ley. May I ask the minister if he is the gentleman who made representations to the minister of that day as to the value of the land?
I do not remember. I know Ldvis just as a traveller would know it, passing through.
The bon. gentleman knew it better than that. I think he knew it as a very fair fee getter.
I do not remember. I have no doubt that if I did the work I charged well for it.

I thought, from the pretty close knowledge the minister had of the locality, as stated in his letter at the time, that he would be able to give us some personal recollections of the locality. I must compliment the minister upon the fact that the land suddenly rose in value from $1 to $2 a foot, and judging from the increase in the price one would naturally conclude that his fee must have been a very fair one. I will refresh the memory of the minister with regard to the matter at some future time. It is on ' Hansard.'
How many years ago was that?
Probably seven or eight years ago.
Many things have happened since then. I do not remember these things for so long a time.
It is a very odd thing that a local solicitor was not called in to make representations to the minister as to the value of this land.
How much money did Mr. Couture receive ?
Up to the first of November the contractor received $26,270. That includes the contract and extras.
Has he a claim now?
Yes, there is $6,266 still owing.
I see in the Auditor General's Report of last year that he received $25,365, and also $3,830; that would be over $29,000 that he has already received.
Yes, he had the contract for heating apparatus as well and the contract for fittings. The contract for fittings amounted to $3,500 and for heating apparatus to $2,178.50.
Did he get all these by tender?
Yes, I see there was an accepted tender dated July 10, 1906.
Who was the clerk of the works?
Mr. Auger.
What was his salary ?
$3 a day.
Did he get paid for Sundays?
I am informed by the chief architect that he was paid for Sundays.
What reason was there for him travelling? 1 see that he received $o2 for travelling.
The chief architect tells me that he summoned him to Ottawa in regard to the foundations.
Was there not an-otner clerk of the works at this time?
I think not.
Was not Mr. Mullar-key also clerk of works?
No, Mr. Mullarkey was attached to the staff at headquarters.
Why was his pay charged up against that work ?
His pay and expenses are charged against the work he inspects.
He is down as having received $4 a day.
During what period?
For 61 days.
We paid his board while he was at Levis. Mr. Mullarkey, I am informed, is an expert on concrete work.
He is the gentleman who supervised the concrete work for the piers of the interprovincial bridge across the Ottawa river.

Then why did he go
to Levis as clerk of works ?
He goes out to places where important work is going on because of his special knowledge of concrete work and his wages are charged to the particular work under construction.
I see that the government has paid his board besides $4 a day.

When he is away from Ottawa, of course his board is paid. He is an expert in concrete work and he is a man whom the chief architect would be justified in sending to Levis if the foundations were as the hon. member who has assisted me in giving information as to the building has stated they were.

Why was it necessary to bring Auger up to Ottawa ? What good would he do ? If there was anything wrong why not send a man down from the architect's department ? He could see with his own eyes what was the matter.
Not being an architect and not being in charge of the work, I would not deem myself competent to criticise the judgment the chief architect exercised.
Would it not be much better judgment to send an architect at first hand to see what was the matter ?

The chief architect tells me that it became necessary to make an arangement with the contractor for the extra work and the clerk of works, Mr. Auger, and the contractor came to Ottawa in order to settle what allowances should be made the contractor.
I would say to the minister as a friend that somebody ought to be watched whether it is the architect or the overseers.
Or the minister.

No, I won't blame him, because he is a new man in the business. All your architect amounts to is just the name ; he tells them what to do and how to do it, and as soon as his back is turned the work is neglected. The investigation into the fall of the tower here proved that the man did not attend to his business at all. Some of these days I will show you a place where some of your men were sent to build a wharf
Was there any water?
Yes, too much of it. The wharf was built and not a stone was put into the wall, and when the ice moved out in the spring away went the wharf, and it will cost $10,000 to replace it.
Where was that ?
I will let you know when the time comes.

As I understand it, while the business portion of L6vis is down near the river side where the post office is situated, the greater part of the town is up the hill. Was it at the suggestion of the municipal authorities that the post office was erected on this site ?
Yes, and the Board of Trade.
The minister has accounted for $11,000 in his own peculiar way, but we want to know something about the remaining $16,000 for extras.

Heating $2,178, tower clock $1,500, fittings $3,500, printing, advertising, clerk of the works, travelling
expenses $4,213, boilers, etc., $196, electric wire $400.
Give the details for each of these items for printing and travelling expenses and advertising.
I have not the details.
How much has the contractor been paid, and how much is due ?
He has been paid altogether $26,270, and $6,226 is still due. The total expenditure to October 31 has been $35,274.44.
Has that beeD paid ?
Yes. The total is $49,715.44.
We are to understand then that this building cost $49,000 ; the contract for which was $22,000 of which sum $7,000 was paid for the clerk of works or one-seventh of the whole amount.
There were two clerks.
Even so.

There must be a
mistake somewhere, because it would appear that most of the accounts mentioned by the minister have been already paid according to the Auditor General's report.
What does the hon. gentleman say has been paid ?

Couture has been
paid $30,000 already ; Auger has been paid, Mullarkey has been paid. The boilers have been paid for, the heaters have been paid for, the King's Printer has been paid.
Have these items been paid, the $6,226 which I say is due ?
No, I do not find that.

The wiring.
Mi-. BERGERON. There is some wiring.
Yes, $400, but there is still $750 due.
Here is a payment to L. F. Butcher, on account of wiring, as per tender, that was a contract.
The wiring and fixtures were not in the contract. Is the $500 for the tower clock paid ?
No.
The $3,500 for fittings ?
No.
The lock boxes, sidewalk and fencing and the balance for contingencies and superintendence, $2,103, making up the total of $49,713.34.
Who was the architect ?
The plans were drawn in the department.
Was there a time limit on the contract ?

The date of the contract is January 31, 1905, and the date named for completion October 30, 1906.
Mr. FOAA'LER. Was it completed then ?
No, owing to the change in site.
Was there a new contract ?
No, but an arrangement was come to with the contractor as to what he should receive for the extras necessitated by the change.
AATien was the arrangement made ?	*
The chief architect says before the changes were made this arrangement was come to as to what he should charge.
Before he did anything, under the changed arrangement the price was agreed on ?

It was by schedule price, so much per cubic yard of concrete and masonry, &c.
Mr. FOWLER, Did the change make any difference in the contract ?
No, ail this very great extra work was by reason of the changed foundation.
Was that the result of the change in the position.

Yes; by putting it back by reason of the widening of the street.
Mi-. FOWLER. That made a difference of how many thousands ?

There is about 75 feet of land between high water mark and the cliff 120 feet high ; that is all the land there is there.
Mr. FOA\rLER. Where Is the building with respect to the street that crosses the railway ?
South east of the railway station.
60 feet from the railway.
Auger was employed at $3 a day. What was his occupation previously ?
He was an architect.
Is it the custom to pay for Sunday on all this work ?

We had a discussion on this on Friday. It has been a pretty general custom. I do not know over how many years the custom has extended, but it has been the general custom to pay inspectors for Sundays.
Did he reside in Quebec?
No, I think he resided in Lfivis.
I). REID. Did he give his whole time to this building ?
I take it for granted he did.

We would like to know. If he is a professional architect and will accept $3 a day and has the ability he should have, I think you should bring him to the department instead of paying architects $50 or $100 a day.
Is the building finished ?
Everything is finished.
From what the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Morin) says it is very serious. It seems the building is shaky.

The member was indulging in figures of speech.
Air. AlORIN. I did not mean that, you say ? I do not blame the present minister but I do blame the government in connection with this matter. They have been 3,J years putting up the building, working for a while and then stopping, and if you paid your architect $3 a day for all the time it is no wonder the building is costing money. Any man can put up a building like that for $10,000 or $12,000. There is no fine work in the building, it is a brick building with stone trimmings around the doors and windows, two storeys high, with a kind of garret and a little tower, probably 50 feet high. I saw them putting in every stone and brick and all the work. The minister said that the wall was resting on concrete but will he state what the concrete rests upon ? He will find out some day that the concrete is not resting on anything solid.

I would like to know if the statement of the hon. gentleman is true that the building

Afr. AlORIN. It is so or I would never say so. If I said it I will stick to it, because I know it to be correct. I will not take back a word of that.
If that statement is true it is very serious. Has the department received any word from Quebec that that is the condition of affairs ? Who has taken the building over ?
I thought my genial friend was joking about the building.
No, I do not joke at all, it is not the place to joke.
The chief architect says he has inspected the building, that it is a good building, that the foundation rests on rock, so it is a solid foundation and the building will last.

Only last year the Minister of Agriculture stated to the House that the total cost would be $42,000. An item of $8,000 for Lgvis public building was under discussion and he stated that $42,000 would finish the work. Now he states it will cost $49,000.

An hon. member from the province of Quebec has stated here tonight that this building rests upon a poor foundation, so poor that the building is already out of plumb at least four inches ; that it shifts with the tide or for some other reason ; that, to use the hon. member for Dorchester's (Mr. Morin) own words, it ' wobbles and warps.' Here is a building on which the government has spent $49,000, including some $7,000 for inspection alone. The government have paid two clerks of work, Mr. Mullarkey and Mr. Auger, one of whom is said to be an architect, paid them for week days and Sundays for about three years to inspect this work. And the chief architect says that he has examined this work and taken it over as all right. Well, here is a great variance of statement. An hon. member from the province of Quebec says he was present when a great deal of the work was done
Has seen every brick put in.
Even if I did, don't poke your nose in.

We hardly hold the hon. member for Dorchester to such exactness of statement as to cover every brick. But he has seen a good deal of the work going on. He lives near there and often sees this building, and taking an interest' in public affairs, as we know he does, he naturally tries to learn what is being done. He makes this statement that this building is not founded on rock
No, I cannot .say that.
Oh, oh.

I am glad to see hon. gentlemen opposite so jubilant. It is so seldom that they get a chance to jubilate Mr. MORIN.
nowadays that we naturally like to see them happy. The hon. gentleman stated that it was on a poor foundation. I took it for granted that that meant it was not upon a rock foundation, as the Minister of Public Works alleged it to be, and I think that that was a fair deduction for me to make from the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Morin's) statement. At any rate, he said-and I think he will stand by that

that it is a poor foundation.
I do not know that anybody knows whether the foundation is good or bad, to come right down to the point.
There is certainly a variation as between the statement of the hon. member for Dorchester and that which the minister reports as the statement of the chief architect.
I think not.

The hon. member for Dorchester says the building is out of plumb, while the minister says it is wTell built. From the fact that so many public buildings put up by this government have fallen, we are naturally suspicious. These buildings collapse mysteriously. As the member for Dorchester has pointed out, even a building on a solid foundation and wedged in between two other parts of a building fell down, though one would naturally have said that such a thing would be impossible. It is no wonder that we incline to take the statements of the chief architect with a grain of salt.

Last summer this building was supposed to be ready to move into. But they were repairing it and they were afraid of it falling down. They only moved in about six weeks ago. I know that perfectly well, because I was in the post office. I wanted to buy a stamp and the postmaster allowed me in, though he said they had not opened yet, but were only moving in that day.
Longueuil public building, $500.
It is past one o'clock, and I would ask the leader of the House (Mr. Fielding) if he does not think it time to quit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have counted up the sums voted and the total is under $100,000.
Well, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) and the Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) have taken up a great part of the evening
Let us sit here as long as they wish.
Sit a reasonable time. We will not stay late. Give us a fair show.

This $500 is to provide for the construction of a retaining wall in

the rear of this building. It is 20 feet long, 8 feet high and 3 feet thick.
This is a new building, is it not?
It was built in 1904.
What do you want with a retaining wall? Is it to keep the building from falling down?
No.
What do you want with a retaining wall if it is not to retain something ?

It is necessary to build a wall at the rear of the grounds-it is far from the building and is not to sustain the building which is perfectly new, well built and a credit to the city and the government.
Then, it is a fence ?
Call it a fence, if you like.
The minister comes down and asks for a vote for a new public building, and now the representative of the county tells us it is a wharf-
No, a wall.
Well, wharf or wall, it is clearly not a public building.

This is in connection with a public building. The improvement of the grounds of a public building would come within these votes. As my hon. friend (Mr. Geoffrion) has explained, it is necessary to build a retaining wall to prevent the earth from falling out.	.
Then, the item should be amended to provide for building a wall and not a public building.
What will happen if you do not build the wall ?
The earth on the lot will fall away.

There is a little rivulet passes there. My hon. friend from Beau-harnois (Mr. Bergeron) and my hon. friend from Laval (Mr. Leonard) know the place very well. It is necessary to build a wall to keep the ground even. It is not a wharf, nor a fence, but a wall.
Who owns the adjoining property ?
I do not know.
How much did the building cost in the first place ?
I have no memo, of that.
Were tenders called for this work ?
Yes, Mr. Baker was the tenderer and the tender was for $950.
I thought this wall was not to cost more than $500.
There was an appropriation in 1907-8 for $1,700, which included also a clock and room for the same.
That is paid for.
Yes, and there were other items making a total of $1,475. Prior to March 31, the expenditure was $975, leaving $500, for which a vote is now asked.
Did you have a clerk of works ?	[DOT]
No.
Who inspected the job ?
One of the resident clerks of works in Montreal.
Is the work finished ?

There is a little something still to be done.
Magog public building, $13,000.

This is a re vote.	The
appropriation last year was $13,000, of which nothing has been expended. The site has been chosen, we paid for it $4,100, to Messrs.
H.	N. Rivard and A. Tourigny. The original lot was 100 feet by 8 feet, for which we paid $3,200. Later on there was purchased another strip from the town of Magog to round out the first lot. For the second strip we paid $900.
What will be the total cost of the building when completed, including furnishings ?

The estimated cost is $22,000 ; this is to include everything outside the lot.
Marieville public building, $7,500.

This is in the county of Rouville. The population of Marieville, including Ste. Marie de Monnoir, is 2,360. The contract has not yet been let. The building will serve for a post office and custom house. The postal revenue for the last nine months was $1,020. and the customs duties $10,939.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow?

speechtext: Supply, at the point where we leave it to-night.
